1. **`playbookKeyFor` (js/playbook.js).** It lowercases the type and runs four
   passes: the workspace's own books' match words, the built-in type patterns,
   a read-but-unmatched type taking the baseline, and finally the value-stream
   fallback for a type nobody read. `copilotPlaybookKey` on the server mirrors
   it pass for pass and **f133 runs both over the same contracts and requires
   the same key.** So this string is not only printed — it is matched on, by
   two hosts, and a wrong answer is silent.
2. **The other two screens that draw this field.** `openMetaReview` (the
   extraction review) and the upload confirm both branch on `f.type==='select'`
   and otherwise draw a text box. Changing the type would have turned both into
   closed dropdowns that DROP a reading off the list — a silent data loss on
   the two screens whose whole job is showing you what Copilot read.
3. **`cKind` (js/core.js).** `TEMPLATES[c.template]?.kind` — twelve words, one
   per built-in template, already written onto every drafted contract.

### THE THREE DECISIONS THAT CAME OUT OF THAT

**THE FIELD STAYS FREE TEXT ON THE RECORD.** It gains `picks`, which means
"free text, and here are words to offer". The type is untouched, so the
extraction review and the upload confirm are byte-identical, and a reading off
the paper can still be corrected there in any words at all. `ovMetaBoxHtml`
gets a third branch, asked before the closed-list one.

**THE WORDS ARE ENGLISH, AND THIS IS THE OPPOSITE OF THE PARTY ROLE BESIDE
IT.** The party role build the day before offered eighteen translated words
(`py_rw_*`) and stored the one the reader picked, and that was right: a party's
role word is what THE PAPER calls them, and a Swedish contract says
"Leverantör". This one is a matching key. A Swedish workspace storing
"Leverantörsavtal" would match none of `playbookKeyFor`'s patterns, fall to
pass 3, and be judged by the baseline book instead of the supply book — with
nothing on any screen saying so. So the offered words stay English, which is
the same ruling `RELATION_DOC_WORD`, `ROLE_LABEL` and the audit lines already
follow: a label that is also a RECORD keeps English. The two screen sentences
that are NOT the record — the last row's own words and the name box's hint —
are translated as usual.

**THE TWELVE ARE READ OFF `TEMPLATES`, NEVER TYPED HERE.** `contractTypeKinds`
walks the template table for its kind column; `CONTRACT_TYPE_FALLBACK` is the
literal for a stage without js/templates.js, written the way `docLibWording`
carries its own fallback wording, and pinned as a no-drift wall against the
table it mirrors. That makes the offered words the SAME words `cKind` writes
onto every drafted contract, which is what lets an uploaded contract and a
drafted one spell one type one way and resolve to one playbook.

And that claim was measured rather than asserted. Staged the way f133 stages
it — `playbookKeyFor` asks `contractTypeRead` and `CKIND_SAYS_NOTHING`, which
live in js/core.js and are not on the playbook world, so a mirror test
measuring the fallbacks measures the wrong thing — every one of the twelve was
run through the real rule on an upload with no template and no value stream:

    Raw Material Supply      -> supply        Distributor            -> supply
    Packaging Supply         -> supply        Retail Listing         -> supply
    Contract Manufacturing   -> supply        Marketing Services     -> services
    Equipment Lease          -> lease         NDA                    -> nda
    Warehousing              -> supply        Lease                  -> lease
    Distribution Logistics   -> supply        Professional Services  -> services

Not one falls through to `_default`, and the control beside it — the same
contract with nothing read — still does. That table is the whole case for the
English choice, and f361 (2) is it written down.

### IT OFFERS AND NEVER REFUSES

The value-stream picker's own mechanism, in four parts:

- **The blank leads**, because clearing a term is an answer — the rule the
  closed-list branch twelve lines below already states.
- **Whatever is on the record leads the words** where it is not one of them,
  folded free of case, so a reading of "Master Services Agreement" is never
  quietly replaced by opening the box. This is the claim a blank record cannot
  measure, which is why the browser check stages an off-list reading first.
- **The last row types the document's own words** through `promptNewName`,
  which is one name box with two consumers already.
- **`metaPickOptions` is the one reading behind all three**, so a second
  `picks` field tomorrow cannot drift from this one.

### A SENTINEL NEVER REACHES THE RECORD, AND THE WALL IS IN THE HANDLER

The party editor is a dialog with a Save button, so its sentinel wall sits at
Save. This grid has no Save: every box writes as it is answered. So the wall is
inside the handler — a cancelled name box returns before anything is written
and puts the value back, exactly as `bindFolderSelect` puts a value stream
back. The browser check drives that cancel and reads the record afterwards.

And **the event is the element's**. The one `[data-ktm]` handler picked its
event from `f.type` alone; a `picks` field is text on the record and a SELECT
on the screen, and a select answers on `change`. Asked of the tag, so the two
cannot disagree.

### THE SIX QUESTIONS

Run, because this moves something a person can press. Q1: a controlled list
with an escape to free text is the standard answer and is what was built. Q2:
the fact sits on the control itself — no band, no line added. Q3: the Overview
is not the agreement's paper and nothing on the contract moved. Q5: the edit
posture already IS the door onto this field, so this improves the one door
rather than adding a second; `promptNewName` is the product's own name box.
Q6: a picked word lands on the record with confidence 'high' exactly as typing
did, and the read-out beside it prints the same word. No refusal bit.

### TWO INSTRUMENT FAULTS, AND A DEFECT THAT IS NOT THIS REQUEST

The first draft of the browser check pressed `Edit these details` and found no
boxes at all — and the same happened at the parent, on a contract with nothing
unusual on it. Traced: `Edit these details` is wired inside `renderKeyTerms`,
which the section router calls on every fold, so on a FIRST paint of the
Overview that act is drawn, hit-testable and does nothing until some fold
repaints the card. Every earlier section of that file happens to fold something
before it presses, which is why it had never been seen. Reported as one line in
BUGLOG — it is not this request — and section 14 folds the card the way the
product's own door does.

And f351 (5) pinned `f.type==='text')?'input':'change'` as a literal source
line. Re-pointed in place to the relation; on the way, its first draft read the
FIRST `const evt=` in `wireKeyTerms`, which belongs to the four fields with a
home of their own. **PIN THE REGION** — the metadata sweep's own — paid again.

## THE OVERVIEW'S ACTS WORK ON A FIRST PAINT (Young ruled 22 Sep 2026)

Young, 22 September 2026: *"fix the edit button bug too."* The bug was the one
line left in the previous run's BUGLOG under "Noticed, not fixed": on a first
paint of the Overview, `Edit these details` did nothing.

### WHAT WAS MEASURED

Driven in a real browser on an ordinary contract — Under Review, a template,
metadata on the record — arriving on the Overview tab for the first time:

    FIRST PAINT:  edit act drawn: 1 · press -> 0 boxes
    AFTER A FOLD: edit act drawn: 1 · press -> 24 boxes

The button was drawn, visible, hit-testable and dead. Folding any section shut
and open again — which is what every other check in that browser file happens
to do before it presses anything — woke it. That is why it had gone unseen
through every run since the Overview was built.

Two further facts from the same measurement:

    slots on first paint: { lead: 50, terms: 5827, side: 899, sideSecs: 2 }

`#kt-ov-lead` and `#kt-side` were FILLED on a first paint — so the tab's own
branch in `applyWsTabs` really does run on arrival, and `renderKeyTermsSide`
really does paint its two hosts. Only the middle one was different.

### THE CAUSE

The Overview's stack is three hosts:

    <div class="ov-stack" id="kt-overview">
      <div id="kt-ov-lead" class="empty:hidden"></div>
      <div id="kt-ov-terms">${ktOverviewTermsHtml(c, …)}</div>   <-- this one
      <div id="kt-side"></div>
    </div>

Two empty slots and one that filled itself. And `renderKeyTerms` — the painter
that would have filled the third — is where EVERY door on that card is wired:

    wireKtRows(c); wireKeyTerms(c);            // the rows, and the boxes
    host.querySelectorAll('[data-ov-edit]')    // Edit these details
    participantsWire(peopleHost, …)            // the people list
    host.querySelector('[data-ov-signers]')    // the signers row
    host.querySelectorAll('[data-ov-fix]')     // a marked field's Fix
    host.querySelectorAll('[data-ov-move-stream]')  // Move to another stream

So the markup arrived and none of it was armed. The tab branch had ONE of
those six patched in by hand —

    if(_wsTab==='terms'){ renderKeyTermsSide(c); if(window.wireKtRows) wireKtRows(c);
      if(window.wireKtParties) wireKtParties(c); }

— which is the tell. Somebody had found the rows dead, armed that one by name,
and the other five stayed dead. Only `Edit these details` is drawn in an OPEN
section on an ordinary contract, so only `Edit these details` was reported.

### THE FIX WAS ALREADY WRITTEN DOWN, TWELVE LINES ABOVE THE FAULT

Immediately above the stack, in the same template:

    ${''/* A SLOT, NOT THE STRIP ITSELF. The room is rendered BEFORE the
           readings run … so interpolating the strip here draws nothing
           and leaves no element for the paint to replace. The product's own
           answer to exactly this is a slot and a painter (#ws-tabrow-end). */}
    <div id="kt-triage-slot"></div>

Same shape, same answer. `#kt-ov-terms` becomes an empty slot, `renderKeyTerms`
fills it, and the tab branch calls it beside the sibling painter it already
called. The host goes from TWO writers to ONE — the change removes a writer
rather than adding a call.

There is no flash: `applyWsTabs(c)` is the last statement of `wireWsTabs(c)`,
so the template's write and the painter's run in the same synchronous tick and
the browser never paints between them. Measured after the change, the host is
5,827 characters on a first paint exactly as before.

### THREE THINGS THAT HAD TO BE GOT RIGHT

**THE STANDALONE `wireKtRows` CALL IS DELETED, NOT MOVED.** `renderKeyTerms`
calls it itself, and `wireKtRows` walks `[data-kt-row]` document-wide adding a
listener per row **with no bound-once flag**. Leaving both calls on the same
path would have put two handlers on every row — and the second handler on a
`.kt-field` blur writes the record a second time.

**ORDER IS LOAD-BEARING.** The side is painted first and the middle second, so
the painter's document-wide row sweep covers whatever the side drew. Written
the other way round, any row `renderKeyTermsSide` paints would be unwired.

**`wireKtParties` SURVIVES THE REPAINT BY CONSTRUCTION.** It is delegated on
the HOST rather than on its children and carries `host.dataset.pyBound`, and
`renderKeyTerms` writes the host's `innerHTML` rather than replacing the
element — so the listener outlives every repaint and the flag still binds it
once. Driven both ways rather than reasoned: `+ Add a party` opens the editor
on a first paint and after a repaint.

Two template locals (`ktEditable`, `ktReadable` at the room's scope) were
orphaned by the change and went with it. `locked` beside them is still read,
and the lint warning set was diffed against the parent and is identical.

### THE CHECKS, AND WHERE THEY HAD TO GO

`overview-as-drawn-verify` gained **section 0**, and its position is the claim:
every other section in that file folds something before it presses, and a fold
is precisely what used to hide this. It presses once, asserts boxes appeared,
presses again to leave the card resting, and section 1 below measures exactly
what it measured before. At the parent `0a` prints `0 boxes before, 0 after` —
the owner's report, reproduced.

`0b` (the press is still a toggle) was written ungated and PASSED at the
parent — on the fault, because nothing had opened so nothing needed closing.
It is gated on `after > 0` now. `0c` (the parties door) passes on both sides
and is LABELLED a control: it is the door this change could most plausibly
have broken, and its job is to say it did not.

f362 pins the structure: the host is a slot, all three in the stack are slots,
`ktOverviewTermsHtml` has exactly one caller, the branch paints the middle host
after the side, `wireKtRows` is called once on that path, and the two `[wall]`
claims that the painter still refuses a missing host and still arms all four
acts. **Two order claims were written with a bare `indexOf` comparison and
passed at the parent**, because an ABSENT call indexes at -1 and -1 sits before
everything; both are gated on the call being present now.

And the note in `overview-as-drawn-verify` section 14 that recorded this
defect as reported-not-fixed was re-pointed in place. A note describing a
defect that no longer exists is worse than no note.

## THE RUNWAY — THE DECISION CARD IS A LINE OF TIME (Young ruled 22 Sep 2026)

It began as five renders. Young asked for the *Needs your decision* card drawn
"more graphic than writings", chose the runway, and then asked the question
that decided the whole shape of the thing:

> *"in idea 1, how does the app measure that dates of redline answers that are
> pending? Redlines usually do not have due dates."*

MEASURED OUT OF THE RECORD RATHER THAN ANSWERED FROM MEMORY, and he is right.
The six readings behind that card hold these dates and no others:

| row | what is stored | what the number meant |
|---|---|---|
| a quiet desk | `createdAt` on their oldest pending change | WORKING days since they asked |
| sitting in review | `c.lastAction` | calendar days since anything happened |
| a review asked of you | `rv.at`, and an OPTIONAL `rv.due` | days since — plus a real deadline, if typed |
| renew or exit | `renewalDecisionDate` | calendar days REMAINING |
| your signature | nothing at all | — |
| a join request | `req.at` | days since |

So "37 days" was never lateness. It was 37 working days since they asked — about
seven and a half calendar weeks — and it sat in the same column as "in 9 days",
which is calendar days remaining. Two units and two directions, printed as one.

THREE RULES CAME OUT OF THAT and they are what js/runway.js is. One unit, and it
is calendar days: the staleness THRESHOLD stays in working days, deliberately,
so a Friday ask is not called stale on Monday, but the distance drawn is a plain
difference between two days and nothing here converts between them. The
left-hand clock starts where the workspace's own answering standard ran out,
never where they asked — a thing is not "45 days late", it is 45 days past a
promise this workspace made to itself, and the rail's own label names it. And a
row with no date is not plotted at all; it is counted beside the rail, and each
count is a door.

THE STANDARD IS THE DESK'S OWN — `deskCfg().staleDays`, five working days by
default, already an admin setting on the negotiation-desk panel and already
published. Reading it rather than inventing a second one means there is one
promise, said in one place, and the quiet-desk flag and the rail cannot come to
disagree about what it is.

WHAT WENT WRONG ON THE DAY, and it is the fault this codebase keeps paying for:
the rail landed and the row beside it still read "42 days" while the dot sat
where the rail puts 53. Both numbers were true. Together they read as a
contradiction twelve pixels apart. The row's tag on this card takes the rail's
own reading now.

THE OWNER EXCLUDED THE EXPLAINER BY NAME — *"you have explanations between the
top card and the paper so please exclude that from the implementation"* — so the
prototype's paragraph is not built. The two end labels carry the two directions,
the left one carries the standard, and where that standard is SET rides the
hover, because Team & settings is the one door onto it.

## X-RAY — THE SWITCH'S THIRD POSITION (Young ruled 22 Sep 2026)

*"Build the X-ray next to plain english."* Contract View shows the paper. Plain
English shows the paper and a translation beside it. X-ray shows the paper, a
map of it down the margin, and everything already known about whichever clause
you are looking at.

IT SPENDS NOTHING, and that is what makes it a POSITION rather than a feature
with a bill. Every section of its panel is a reading this product has already
paid for: the plain-English entry out of the `_readings` the second position
wrote, paired by that position's own anchors; the open risk-scan findings; the
playbook review's verdicts; and the clause ladder. X-ray adds no route, no store
and no field — it is a third way of LOOKING at what is there.

THE MAP BELONGS IN A MARGIN, AND THE MARGIN IS GREY, NEVER PAPER. The sheet is
capped at `--doc-sheet-max` and centred, so there is page ground either side of
it whenever the column is wider than the sheet. The spine floats over that
ground: nothing in the layout changes, so the contract cannot move by a pixel —
refusal 3 satisfied by construction rather than by argument, and then measured
anyway, inside the document, identical before and after. Where the ground is too
narrow the spine is not drawn and the panel still works.

TWO NUMBERS WERE WRONG ON THE FIRST BUILD. A 34px map wanting 10px of clearance
did not fit the 43px of grey an ordinary 1500px window leaves, and missed by ONE
pixel — it drew nothing, silently. And the segments were neutral-300 on a
neutral-100 ground, 1.1:1, so the map read as an empty strip. Both were found by
looking at a rendered page rather than at the source.

THE STORE KEPT ITS KEY. What was a yes/no about one layer is now which layer,
and `'1'` still means Plain English, so a browser holding yesterday's choice
opens where it always did. `docReadOn()` keeps its name and its answer, said in
terms of the mode, which is what stops its six existing callers drifting from it.

AND THE ORDER IS LOAD-BEARING: `docXrayPaint` runs after `docReadPaint`
everywhere the mode or the tab changes, because that painter correctly hands
`#doc-right` back whenever the edition is off — which, in this mode, it is. Two
writers of one property only agree while one of them runs last.

### FORMAT A — THE MAP IS GRADED, AND THE READING IS HANDED OVER (Young ruled 22 Sep 2026)

The morning after X-ray shipped, two screenshots off an iPad:

> *"Image 1, the x ray says press in plain english to get a plain English but plain english is already there and also when i press on plain english nothing happens. Image 2, the brief addresses concerns, unusual clauses and areas i should pay attention to in the contract but these clauses are not highlighted in the x-ray. Bring consistency to the platform so that people can have confidence in and seamless review of the contract. Bring the areas I should pay attention to to the xray in the event i missed reading the brief. They should obvisouly have different color gradings but create a format that makes sense. Also, place lines dividing the contract, plain english and x-ray Buttons. Do not code but create an artifact with proposals."*

Three formats were drawn and put to him. He answered: **"I want format A button D1"**.

#### BOTH FAULTS WERE MEASURED BEFORE A LINE MOVED

A scratchpad probe drove the real page, staged a complete thirteen-clause reading on a real contract, and read the answers back:

```
STAGED A READING   {"rows":13,"items":13,"itemsOnRecord":13,"readSig":"undefined","sigNow":"13:1ibuctd"}
FAULT A            anchors_withItems: 13 · anchors_asXrayCallsIt: 0
                   panelPlainSection: "IN PLAIN ENGLISH No reading of this clause yet. Press Plain English to have one made."
FAULT B            before {mode:"paper", readSig:"undefined", items:13}
                   askedTheRoute: 1
                   after  {mode:"paper", layerHidden:true, plainLit:"false"}
                   itemsStillOnRecord: 13
```

**Fault A is one missing argument.** `docReadAnchors(c, items)` takes the entries as its SECOND parameter and walks `(items||[])`. The panel called it `docReadAnchors(c)`, so it walked an empty list, found nothing, and printed the only sentence it has for that case. It had never once worked — that sentence had appeared on every clause of every contract since the day the X-ray shipped.

**And the check that should have caught it was asserting the defect.** f364 (4) required the literal `docReadAnchors(c)`; the browser file opened a contract that had no reading and asked whether the panel said "no reading", which passes either way. Both are reversed in place, with the reasoning kept beside them — a check that passes against the broken build is a description, not a test, and this file has now paid for that lesson in three different costumes.

**Fault B is one field read two ways.** `c._readSig` is written in exactly one place, inside `docReadRun`, and it is neither stored, nor transport, nor on the payload — so it lives only as long as the tab. `c._readings` beside it rides every GET. After a refresh the app therefore holds a whole edition and no memory of what it was written about, and `c._readSig !== sig` read that absence as *the wording has changed*. Every page load, the first press bought a reading it already had; and `if(!await docReadRun(c)) return;` abandoned the press before `docViewSet(mode)`, so any refusal — no key, the day's cap, a slow link — showed the reader nothing at all.

`docReadPaint`, 250 lines down, had been reading the same field correctly since the day it was written: `sig && c._readSig && c._readSig !== sig`. Two readings of one fact, disagreeing, which is this codebase's own most expensive fault class. They agree now.

#### THE THREE GRADES, AND WHY THEY COULD BE READ AT A GLANCE

The grades were not invented for this. Every one of them is a colour this product already uses for that meaning, which is the whole reason three of them can be read without being learned:

| Grade | Means | Already drawn this way in |
|---|---|---|
| **Ruby** | This could hurt you | the X-ray's own high findings |
| **Amber** | Worth a look before you sign | the brief's watchouts (19 Aug), a playbook departure on the negotiate page |
| **Steel** | Worth knowing, not a warning | the brief's unusual terms, in its own quiet grey |
| **no mark** | Nothing on the record mentions this clause | *said in words, because silence must never read as approval* |

`XR_GRADES` is `['ruby','amber','steel']` and **the order IS the rank**: `docXrayTone` walks it and takes the first that any mark wears, so "a clause wears its worst mark, never its first" holds by construction rather than by a chain of tests. `XR_SEV_GRADE` maps the scan's own `high`/`med`/`low` and is the only thing in the file that hands out ruby.

Three is the ceiling, and the sheet is the net: exactly three `.doc-xr-seg.is-*` rules, and `is-high` is stale with nothing dressing it and nothing building it.

#### THE BRIEF'S TWO LISTS ARE NOT THE SAME KIND OF THING

Measured off the schema on the server, which is what decided the design:

- `watchouts[]` — up to six, `{point, quote}`, `required: ['point']`. **The quote is optional but usually there**, and the prompt asks for one continuous verbatim passage. So a watchout can be placed on its clause with certainty, by the very containment `docXrayPlace` already insists on for a risk finding.
- `unusual[]` — up to four, **a bare string**. No wording at all.

So `docXrayMarks` reads the watchouts and **does not read the unusual list**, and that absence is load-bearing. Pinning a sentence to a clause by matching its words is the product guessing, and a note beside the wrong clause is worse than no note. Three answers were put to the owner and he took the first: say them about the whole contract.

`docXrayWide(c, rows)` is that block. It carries the unusual terms in steel, plus any watchout whose wording did not land on a clause — and **drops one that did**, so nothing is said twice. `docXrayBriefWatch` is the one reading of the list with exactly two askers, so the clause marks and the contract-level block cannot disagree about what is in it.

`docXrayMarkHtml` is the ONE builder for a mark wherever it is drawn. Every mark names its source, so amber never hides whether this is a rule of yours or something the paper itself does.

#### D1, AND WHY IT IS BETWEEN EVERY PAIR

Three treatments were drawn at real size, each in two states, because the only real question is what a divider does when it meets the filled half:

- **D1** — a hairline between every pair, the frame's own `--accent-ink` at 45%. On white it is a light hairline; where it meets the fill the fill shows through it as a slightly deeper shade. Either way it reads as a seam.
- **D2** — dividers only between the unlit halves. Tidier at rest, and **the rules move as the lit half moves**, which is the one thing this product does not do.
- **D3** — a full-strength rule. Reads as three buttons in a box rather than one control in three parts.

He took D1. It is one declaration, `.doc-read-seg button + button`, at (0,1,2) against the base rule's (0,1,1), so it wins on weight and needs no override of last resort. The `aria-pressed` rule is (0,2,1) and sets no border, so there is no contest. MEASURED after: the group is still 30px against a `--ctl-h` of 30.

#### WHAT THE CHECKS NOW STAGE

The browser file's new section 7 exists because section 4 did not: it opened a contract with **no** reading, **no** brief and **no** scan. Section 7 stages a reading per painted row, a brief whose first watchout quotes real wording and whose second carries none, two unusual terms, and a high plus a low finding on two different clauses — then measures the painted panel, the graded spine, the press with the route refusing, and the dividers with the last half lit.

Against unmodified main it prints the owner's screenshot back:

```
· 7a the panel shows the reading that is ON the record — "No reading of this clause yet. Press Plain English to have o"
· 7i Plain English opens off the reading already on file, buying nothing — {"asked":1,"mode":"paper","hidden":true,"notes":0}
· 7j D1 — a hairline between every pair, none before the first — [0,0,0]
```

Two instrument faults were found and fixed on the way, both of them the quiet kind: a grade sweep that counted `.doc-xr-seg.is-on` as a fourth grade, and a call count that matched its own function declaration. Two more browser claims passed **vacuously** at the parent (an absence in a block that is not drawn; "the lit one is the first one" on a build with no dividers at all) and are gated now.

## THE UPLOADED CONTRACT, FIXED — A TO L (Young's go, 22 Sep 2026, over "HaTi — The Uploaded Contract, Fixed")

The owner uploaded a real Maersk SaaS agreement (a 340 KB Word file, 200,000 characters) and reported, over a morning of screenshots: most clauses drawn as big bold headings; Plain English refusing to finish; the X-ray not showing the risk scan, its map grey with one amber segment and every concern "bunched together" at the foot; the obligations tile landing on an empty tab when 73 had been found; no reason given for any concern; and three Overview cards out of line. He asked for a diagnosis without code, then for a drawing of every fix, then "go ahead with A to L".

**ONE CAUSE UNDER THE FIRST THREE.** Lawyers' templates number their clauses with Word's own heading styles — "Heading 2" is how Word numbers 1.1, 1.2 — and write the whole clause in that paragraph: a bold run-in title, then the wording. The reader decided "heading" from the style alone (`docxHeadingStyles` marks any style with an outline level), so 310 paragraphs became `<h*>`, 142 of them longer than 25 words. The paper drew them in the heading's size and weight. Plain English sent each as a SECTION with nothing under it, and the route tells the model in capitals that a section's reading is EMPTY — so the column stayed white beside them. And the X-ray matched every quote against a row's `text`, which for a heading row is only what follows it, so no concern could land on those clauses: the map stayed grey and everything fell to the contract-level list.

**WHY THE RULE IS THREE SIGNS AND NOT A LENGTH.** A length alone misses the short list items ("the Services fail to satisfy Supplier's warranties; or" — Heading 5 in that file) and a punctuation rule alone would take "1. Definitions." So: a run-in bold title followed by wording; or a sentence/list ending with at least four words; or more than twenty words. A short unpunctuated heading stays a heading, which is what every other file relied on. The step class comes from the file's OWN outline level, before the title shift — the first cut used the shifted level and pushed every clause one step in.

**THE PLAIN ENGLISH SAFETY NET IS FOR CONTRACTS ALREADY UPLOADED.** Re-read document fixes a stored body, but it refuses an edited or sealed one; so the sheet walk itself treats a heading-only row that is wording by the same measure as a clause carrying its own words. That moves the sent shape for those rows only, once. A second finding: Word splits one bold title into many runs ("Request ", "for ", "provision of" …) and `_docReadBoldLead` read only the first `<strong>`, so the printed heading was "Request". It now joins adjacent bold siblings, and accepts a title that starts straight after the clause's own number.

**THE BLANK COLUMN WAS ALSO A SILENCE.** The partial and cap lines are drawn at the edition's FOOT. On a sixty-page contract that is a thousand lines below where the reader is looking, so "refused to finish" looked like nothing at all. The same sentence and the same Read again now ride the head, in the moved line's slot — no band.

**THE X-RAY DROPPED WHAT IT COULD NOT PLACE — BUT ONLY FROM TWO OF ITS FOUR SOURCES.** Brief items that landed nowhere were said in About this contract; scan findings and playbook verdicts simply vanished. And a MATCHING playbook verdict was drawn amber, because the X-ray refused `'ok'` and the route answers `'aligned'`. One mark builder per source now, shared by the clause list and the contract-level block, sorted worst first.

**THE UNUSUAL WALL IS REVERSED, NARROWLY.** The X-ray's own section said an unusual term "carries a sentence and no wording, so there is no clause it can honestly be pinned to". True then — the schema gave it nothing else. The brief now asks for a quote on every unusual term, so one that carries a quote places by exactly the watchouts' containment; one that does not still stays contract-level and is never matched by its words.

**THE REASON.** The owner asked for a "why" after every concern. Scan findings already carried one; the brief did not, so its schema requires `why` on watchouts and unusual terms and the ceiling moved from 4,000 to 6,000 by the note's own arithmetic. Older briefs are read both ways and draw no reason line until rewritten — not rewritten automatically, because each rewrite is a charge.

**THE OBLIGATIONS TILE.** It always went to the tab. The 73 were held on the arrival reading waiting to be ticked, so the tab was empty. `runFindObligations` already offers a held reading without charging; the tile now asks one reading — tab empty and something held → the list; otherwise the tab.

**THE THREE CARDS, MEASURED.** Who else: `sectionHtml` leaves the body inset to its caller and this caller gave none — text and button at 1px from the card edge against every other card's 17. What Copilot read: the table's head row started at 0px under the card's head rule. Parties: the first row's own top rule sat 2px under the head's rule; the rule that removed it was written for `.py-item`, which went on 22 Sep.

Proved against the parent: f366 24 of 26 red there, uploaded-contract-fixed-verify 14 of 19 red there (the parent's screenshot shows "[object Object]" for a new-shape unusual term — the reason the brief panel reads both shapes).

## SIGNING WITHOUT THE FACTS — THE THREE QUICK FIXES (Young's go, 23 Sep 2026)

**THE ASK.** Over a screenshot of the Overview's deal card with half its cells dashed: *"It seems it is possible to sign a contract without filling in some necessary information from the deal card and other fields in the overview page. Please review, summarize the gaps and advise how we can close the gaps effortlessly or seamlessly. No coding."* The review was run against the real signing check before anything was said, then four decisions were put back and the owner asked for my recommendations: a must/should split (must = what HaTi needs to work after signing — reminders, money, approvals, the right playbook; should = legal risk the standards check already reviews), must fields BLOCK but always carry an honest one-press answer ("Not in this contract", "On signature", "No end date"), anyone who can edit may give that answer with a reason (only "Non-monetary" over a paper that shows an amount goes to an admin or the named colleague), and blanks are caught at the FIRST SEND as well as at signing. Then: *"Go ahead but start from the latest main"* — the go on the three quick fixes named with them. **The rest of that plan is not built and waits for its own go.**

**WHAT THE SIGN BUTTON ACTUALLY ASKED, MEASURED.** Three things about a contract's content: the counterparty, the value (only where money passes), and bracket or brace placeholders in wording we drafted. A contract set up like the owner's screenshot held NOTHING and listed nothing. The effective date and the expiry were only 'warn' rows — and signReadiness takes blockers, never warnings, so they never reached the signing list at all, only the Send screen's folded "worth checking".

**1 · A VALUE LEFT EMPTY WAS STAMPED "NO MONEY PASSES".** The company-standard route wrote `valueType: Number(b.value) > 0 ? 'estimated' : 'none'`, so a value box the form itself labels "if known", left empty or skipped, made the contract non-monetary for life: isMonetary answered false, the value row never held, the signing cap and value-based approvals had nothing to measure, and the Overview printed "Non-monetary" and greyed its box. PROVED against a real server before a line moved (value typed → estimated; value empty → none; Skip for now → none). No ruling produced it — the route once hardcoded its blanks empty and kept 'none' when the essentials form arrived, "exactly the blanks it produced before". The mailroom did the same to every document it filed, which contradicted its own note ("nothing it creates is a contract anybody has agreed").
- **THE TEMPLATE ANSWERS THE SILENCE, WHERE IT CAN.** Dropping the stamp outright would have made every company-standard NDA ask for a value at signing. The template row carries a category and `nda` is one of the five, so an NDA standard with no value still reads 'none' — the company-standard twin of TEMPLATES.ND — and everything else writes nothing, which isMonetary reads as money (its documented default for a template with no view).
- **THE IMPORTER WAS LEFT ALONE, ON PURPOSE.** It stamps 'none' on a no-value import too, but migNeedsReview reads 'none' as "value not needed" — dropping the stamp would send every imported contract without a readable value to the review queue — and the importer's default status is Signed, where no signature is left to guard.
- **NO BACKFILL.** Records already stamped cannot be told apart from a person's own tick: the only mark a deliberate tick leaves is an audit line, which the LIGHT list strips, so a load-time repair would answer differently on the register and in the room — this file's most expensive fault class — and a server rewrite of stored records is against the grain of every other repair here. The way back is one untick in Edit these details. Put to the owner rather than decided.

**2 · THE EFFECTIVE DATE WAS READ, CONFIRMED AND DROPPED.** applyMetadata — the upload's own confirm — copied the counterparty, the value and the expiry into the record, and left the effective date in `metadata` alone. The Overview's Effective cell reads `c.fields.effDate`, and so do the record check and Copilot's card, while the Term beside it reads `metadata.effectiveDate` as a fallback: two readings of one fact, disagreeing on one card. PROVED in a world: a confirmed 2026-10-01 left the cell empty. The same omission sat in the import queue's confirm and the import re-read; only Fill from document had the copy.
- **ONE HELPER, `metaEffDateOnto`, FOUR CALLERS**, so a fifth door is one call. An ISO day or nothing (the ktDayDot lesson — a model answering "1 October 2026" would otherwise land in a date box). Fill only; `overwrite` for the import queue's confirm alone, because that function already overwrites the expiry beside it with the value a person just confirmed.
- **THE IMPORTER'S BUILD IS NOT A CALLER.** Paper executed elsewhere is sealed the moment it lands (EXECUTED_IMMUTABLE freezes `fields`), and an unconfirmed machine reading written there could never be corrected. A working import takes the date when a person confirms it.

**3 · AN EMPTY BOX IN OUR OWN PAPER WAS SIGNED AS A DASH.** readOnlyDocHtml and freezeContractHtml turn an empty template input into "—", and the placeholder pattern only ever matched `[CAPS]`, `{{key}}` and `____`. MEASURED on all twelve built-in templates: a fresh draft carries the start date plus one or two core boxes (Material, Territory, Premises, Services…) — never an optional one — and a Raw Material Supply contract under review with two empty boxes signed with nothing in the way.
- **A BLOCK, NOT A NEW GATE.** The Send screen already asks a tick for a block and signBlockers already holds on one, so the row joins READINESS_FIELD_KEYS as `blanks` and both doors know what to do. `contractBoxesOpen` is the fill panel's own reading narrowed to kind `field`, so the panel's N of M, the Send screen and the Sign button cannot name different boxes.
- **THE DOOR HAD TO BE CHOSEN, because past Draft the panel is gone** (docFillable) and "Open the document" would land on a dash nobody can type into. Draft → the fill panel, cursor in the first box; past Draft, where every empty box is one the Overview owns (the start date — the same `c.fields.effDate`) → that cell; otherwise the negotiation, where words are proposed. Its own attribute: `data-sc-nego` is bound with querySelector, so a second one under the negotiation row would have been dead (f295's lesson).
- **ONE FACT, SAID ONCE.** Where the empty box is the start date, the old "No effective date is recorded" warning stood beside the block on one screen; it stands down now.
- **THE OVERVIEW MARKS THE BOX IT OWNS**, through the 21 Sep machinery (signFieldMarks) — the owner's standing ruling that a field holding the signature is marked where the field is.

**FOUND ON THE WAY, LOGGED, NOT FIXED** (proved at unmodified main): the Document tab keeps its canvas from the last full paint, so a term typed on the Overview reaches a built-in contract's paper on the next paint of the room, not on a tab switch; the import queue's confirm on an import executed elsewhere is refused by the server (409, `metadata` is immutable after execution); signBlockMessage's tail still says "Key terms".

Proved against the parent: f367 13 of 21 red there (the eight that pass are named controls and walls); signing-without-the-facts-verify 21 of 26 red there — the parent prints `Sign as Amina Otieno` over two empty boxes and opens the signature pad, sends the draft with no tick, and ticks "Non-monetary" on a skipped value.

**THE BROWSER SET, COMPARED FILE BY FILE.** The whole set ran once on this branch (45 of 136 red) and every red file was run again beside a worktree at unmodified main, failure names compared. Four were this change's own, and all four were FIXTURES, not faults: each staged a contract drafted from a built-in template with its boxes never filled, so it now carries the `blanks` hold the owner asked for. sign-links-verify's "once nothing blocks" claim and signing-flow-verify's every count ("Sign — 3 to settle" where 1 was owed) were measuring a row they are not about — both now fill the boxes through `contractBlankSet` in their staging, and BEFORE the wording is hashed, because the boxes are part of the wording the check's stamp is taken against (signing-flow-verify already carried the identical note for the brief). signers-and-party-verify's MK-SP1 filled its start date and not its `material`, so the Send screen asked its tick before the signer rule could speak — the fixture now fills both. nda-carries-no-money-verify pinned "2 things to fix" on an RM fixture and now asks the relation it is named for. Every other red file failed identically at main.

## WHO DOES WHAT — THE X-RAY'S THIRD SECTION, AND ONE LIGHT-RED AREA (Young ruled 25 Sep 2026)

**What was asked.** Two screenshots of the X-ray. On the first, the owner ringed the per-clause *Worth a look* list and wrote: *"right below the plain english subsection, i want this highlighted area in the x-ray page to be the area that is highlighted in light red."* On the second he ringed *About this contract · 6*: *"this 'about contract x' portion should be excluded from the x-ray so there is only one red highlighted area which is the worth a look area."* Then, before anything was built: *"Before you start … delete this red … which will leave an empty space in the page. Advise what I can add there … provide 3 options. It should not be something that will be constant every time you move to a different clause like 'about contract x' currently appears."*

**The three options (artifact "X-ray Panel Options").** Each drawn on the real Document-tab page, full size, one at a time with a switcher, over the owner's own Article XIV and the indemnity clause from his screenshots:
1. *Who does what* — what the clause makes each side do, may do, and what it limits, by side, ticked where the Obligations tab already holds it;
2. *Your standard* — the playbook's figures beside this paper's, what you usually settle for, your own wording — no verdict (Worth a look keeps that);
3. *Defined words* — the contract's own meaning for each capitalised word the clause uses, and the parts it points to.
MEASURED coverage on 480 clauses of 38 real agreements from CUAD (The Atticus Project, CC BY 4.0), split at their numbered headings — a rough figure, said so: a duty or a right in 69% of clauses (two or more in 46%); a defined word or a cross-reference in 65% (two or more defined words in 39%); a clause of a kind the default playbook holds a standard for in 26%. *Your standard* was the strongest where it applied and empty on three clauses in four; *Defined words* often had one entry (Article XIV has exactly one). The recommendation was *Who does what*, and the owner took it: *"start from the latest main and build it using your recommendation of who does what. Merge to main once completed."*

**The one light-red area.** The shade *About this contract* had worn since 22 Sep (ruby wash 55% mixed into the surface, a 22% ruby edge, the large radius) moved onto the clause's own *Worth a look*, on a new name `is-look` and only with `has`. The default taken and said on the drawing: **only while it holds something** — a red box saying "nothing here" is an alarm about nothing; the exposure page ruled the same (19 Sep). *About this contract* is no longer drawn. `docXrayWide` was **kept whole with no caller**, the retired-readings precedent (tplHealthData, the ladder's hover card): a reading deleted outright is rebuilt worse, and two lines in the panel put it back. Nothing it listed is lost — the brief, the risk scan and the playbook check still carry every item.

**The reading.** No model, no spend, no route — the duty highlighter's own safety (19 Sep). A DUTY is `DOC_DUTY_RE`, **borrowed** as `new RegExp(DOC_DUTY_RE.source,'i')`: that pattern carries the `g` flag for its painter, and two readers sharing one `lastIndex` is a bug that only shows on the second call. A RIGHT is "may" (or "is entitled to", "has the right to", "reserves the right to") before an action verb from a named list — the list is what keeps "may be", "may have" and "as may be agreed" out — and "may not" is a prohibition. A LIMIT is the handful of phrases that cap or exclude a liability; the pattern asks for *is/are/be* in front of "limited to" because "including but not limited to" is the commonest phrase in drafting and caps nothing. The earliest phrase in a sentence decides it. "Neither party shall disclose" carries its negative in the SUBJECT, so a subject naming *neither* or *no party* turns a duty into a must-not. Sentences split only at an ending followed by a capital or a digit, never after an abbreviation (Inc., e.g.) and never inside a clause number (XIV.2).

**Who.** The order is the one printed on the drawing: (1) words naming BOTH sides in the subject — asked of the subject alone, so "notice to the other party" in the object never makes a one-sided duty mutual — because the Obligations tab records one owner per item and cannot say "both"; (2) an obligation on the tab whose own quote sits in the sentence (containment, the X-ray's rule) answers with its owner, since a person may have ruled on it there; (3) the party's own name: the legal names and role words off `contractParties`, plus the short name the paper defines in brackets right after a legal name — `Highland Corporate Ltd ("Customer")` — with the search stopped at the next party's name so one side's bracket is never read as the other's; (4) otherwise UNCLEAR, and the line then shows the whole sentence, subject and all. **FOUND ON THE REAL PAGE**: "the parties shall cooperate in good faith" is a duty on the tab but *cooperate* is not on the highlighter's (owner-ruled, narrow) verb list, so the first build drew it as "You must · Upon termination or expiration…" — the tab's owner, and the whole sentence. `XR_MODAL_RE` finds the modal in a sentence the tab vouches for, and only there, so its subject can be read (both) and its line can start at the verb.

**The section.** Sorted you · them · both · unclear, the paper's order inside a side. Each line: the chip (a subject and its modal, so a line reads as a sentence — "You must" · "pay each undisputed invoice…"), the contract's own words from the verb, the paragraph's own number, and — where the tab holds it — a green tick with its day. A balance bar and sentence ("You 3 · They 1") head the list. **The chips wear no amber**: in this panel amber already means "worth a look", and a colour with two meanings twelve pixels apart stops being read. **MEASURED**: with each line sizing its own chip, "Either side may" and "Both must" put two lines' wording 30px apart; the section's body is now the grid and each line borrows its three tracks by `subgrid`. Every chip key is written out in full inside a closure — a key built from pieces was invisible to f364's both-books net (it failed on `'xr_wd_'`), and an object of plain strings would freeze the load-time language.

**The presses.** A line press is `scrollToQuote(sentence)` — the risk scan's own "take me to these words", which lights the passage amber and centres it — and the door is `roomGoTab(…,'oblig')`, the one router both shells press, with the contract looked up LIVE by id because `docXrayWire` arms its listener once per element.

**Instrument lessons, paid again.** (1) A REALM MISMATCH: arrays born inside the jsdom world failed `deepStrictEqual` against identical literals; compared as strings. (2) "It is the only red area" PASSED at the parent — the one red area there was *About this contract*; the check now asks WHICH area is red. (3) "XIV.1 is not a line" PASSED at the parent on an empty list; gated on there being lines. (4) The pick helper read `r.heading` off the X-ray's rows, which carry the walk's row under `r.row` — it found nothing and pressed nothing until corrected.

**A reading that throws draws nothing.** The empty state says *"HaTi found nothing in this clause that says who must, may or may not do something"* — a claim about the clause. A fault in the reading is not that claim, so the panel guards the call, logs the fault and draws no section at all.

**Measured.** The contract does not move with the X-ray open (first ink 277.4 / 295.1, sheet 735, before and after). Night: the box reads dark red and every chip stays inked.

## FOUR FIXES OFF ONE LONG CONTRACT (Young's order, 23 Sep 2026)

Three screenshots and one request off the Maersk SaaS agreement, the morning after A–L merged. *"You have made things worse here and we now have errors included in the fields"*; *"hati seems to not be able to read a long contract which is unacceptable"*; *"make the scale scrollable so that the DNA strands are not too tiny to click on"*; and *"i need upload to be inside draft new agreement"*.

**THE FIELDS WERE NOT A.–L.'s, AND WERE STILL OURS TO FIX.** The deal card printed `Terms not specified in available text</paymentTerms><parameter name="value">0` and a governing law carrying the disputes answer after the same seam. That is the metadata reading (`/api/ai/extract`), which A–L did not touch: the model wrote its own call syntax inside a string field, and nothing between the provider and the record looked at what came back. The reading's answer had grown on 21 Sep (three free-text fields) past the 1,500-token ceiling written for eleven. The fix is a wall, not a prompt: one reading (`js/metaclean.js`) asked at the route, at the browser's door, and on the way in, so a record already carrying the fault prints clean without being read again. It recovers only what the model itself wrote under a known field's name, and only into an empty field; it never overwrites an answer and never invents one. An answer that only says the contract is silent is filed as silence, so the card prints its em-dash.

**THE LONG CONTRACT FAILED ON TWO ARITHMETICS, NEITHER A MODEL FAULT.** Pages were sixty CLAUSES; sixty clauses of long commercial paper is ~60,000 characters and its translation does not fit in 8,000 tokens, so the first page came back cut short, was discarded, and the reader was told Copilot had nothing to say. And the whole edition was held to `aiDocChars` — ONE call's ceiling — though every page is its own call, so a contract a little over 200,000 characters lost its last pages and the reader was told the input was shortened. Pages now close on their wording; the whole-edition ceiling is gone; a page still cut short is split and asked again once; and an edition that could not finish says so in its head.

**THE MAP SQUEEZED 200 CLAUSES INTO ONE SCREEN.** Blocks were `flex` shares of the column; each clause got a few pixels. A block is now a height with a floor it can be pressed at, and the strip scrolls and follows the paper.

**UPLOAD MOVED BEHIND THE ONE BUTTON.** The owner chose doors over tabs by leaving the recommendation standing; `openNewAgreement()` called by a person (no options) opens the two doors, and every internal caller passes options and is untouched. Five browser files that pressed the button to reach the drafting screen now press the Draft door, re-pointed in place.


## NINE OFF THE OWNER'S LIST (Young's go, 23 Sep 2026)

**THE THIRD PLAIN ENGLISH REPORT WAS NOT A READING FAULT.** The two before it were: pages too big, a ceiling on the whole edition. This one showed "56 clauses could not be matched" — every page answered, and the server threw the answers away. Each entry had to echo its row's heading exactly after folding case and space. A Word contract's headings carry curly quotes, tabs, long bold lead-ins; the model tidies what it copies; every tidied echo was a refusal, and past a quarter refused the whole edition was not kept. The echo was built to catch a SHIFT (11 Sep: an entry filed under its neighbour's key). So the judge now asks which row the echo describes: its own → paired; another row of the whole list → refused; none → the key decides. And the clauses still unpaired are re-asked by themselves once, so "try again" is HaTi's job, not the reader's.

**THE OTHER EIGHT** were small: the dropdown's own scroll reached a page-scroll listener in the capture phase and shut it; our row had no email because nothing had ever been asked to find one (the owner's address, looked up); the town box went on the owner's word; Who else keeps its hand-named rows and gains a reading of who worked on the contract, drawn and never stored; the Document tab forgot nothing it should have remembered and remembered the one thing it should not; the X-ray map's grey blocks were an absence printed once per clause; Send to counterparty opened the same dialog as Share beside it; the X-ray panel's sizes were tokens that never met the stepper; and the two clean readings went from every switch, their renderers kept.


## SEVEN FIXES OFF ONE REVIEW (Young's go on the before-and-after preview, 23 Sep 2026)

**HOW IT CAME.** Two uploads — a Warehousing and Logistics agreement and a Maersk SaaS agreement — and a list of complaints: wrong clause numbers, words glued together, "Prepare redlines" finding nothing to do on a contract that plainly departed from the standards, a highlight in the parties block that could not be edited, two different-looking Copilots in one editor, Plain English giving up on a long contract, and "Jurisdiction: Sweden" under a Kenyan-law contract. Each was diagnosed first and answered in plain English; the owner ruled on five questions ("1: you are right, do not change two highlighted clauses. 2: … 3: Our standards. 4: OK."; governing law "A, show the governing law the contract names"), asked for a preview page rather than code, approved it, and said *"fix all from 1 through 7 and merge to main."* The Maersk file itself never reached the session; fix 1 was proved on files built to carry both of its shapes.

**1 · WORD'S NUMBERS.** Word numbers a paragraph through a chain HaTi was walking one link of: a paragraph's style names a list, the list is a STYLE-LINKED abstract (`w:numStyleLink`) whose real definition sits under another abstract (`w:styleLink`), and a style inherits its numbering from the style it is `basedOn`. Missing any link printed either no number or the sequence of a different list. Numbered paragraphs inside a table had their own counter, so the body's numbering restarted after every table. Where a list cannot be counted all the way through, HaTi used to print what it had — numbers that were confidently wrong; it now prints none and says so on the file strip, because a wrong clause number on a contract is worse than a missing one. The glued words ("Order.Unless", "agreedService") were a space that Word had put in a bold or underlined run of its own: the sanitiser removed the empty-looking run and the space went with it. It now strips the dress and keeps the space. THE REAL FILE ARRIVED AT THE END OF THE RUN and settled it: the schedule headings are set in a style called "Ikke med" (Danish, "not included" — meant to keep them out of the table of contents), which is based on Heading 1 and overrides nothing, so Word numbers them in Heading 1's own list. Main left them unnumbered and called "Project testing" 48, so every clause under it was nine numbers low ("48.2 Completion of performance of Project Phase" is 57.2 in Word); the branch reads 57.2.

**2 · PAGE BANNERS.** The Warehousing agreement sets "PAGE 1 OF 4: …" as Heading 2 over its clauses as Heading 3. The clause model's rule — headings mark the clauses, at the highest level present — read the four banners as the clauses: 5 clauses where the paper has 12. The shape is recognisable: unnumbered headings above numbered ones whose numbers run ON across them (3, 4, 5 under banner 1, then 6, 7 under banner 2). The banner is kept and drawn — it is the paper's own words — but as a quiet title riding with the clause after it, with no pencil, because nobody negotiates a page banner. The owner's decision that a contract already negotiated keeps its split is what the stamped branch is for: once ids are written into the body, the ids say which headings are clauses, so no later change can flip the reading underneath filed changes.

**3 · EVERY STANDARD.** The review asked only the handful of positions in the book the contract TYPE picked, so a standard on the Our standards page — Termination on the Warehousing contract — was never asked about, and the page promised a check it did not make. And "every position is aligned" was true of an EMPTY list: an answer cut short by its 2,500-token ceiling arrived as no verdicts and was reported as a clean bill. The check now asks one question per standard on the page; the book still says how hard each is held; the ceiling is sized to the number of questions; a cut-short answer is said and refused; "does not apply" is a fourth answer so a clause that is not in this kind of contract is not reported as a gap; and every sentence the reader sees names how many standards were checked, so "nothing to do" can never again be said over nothing.

**4 · ANY HIGHLIGHT.** The recital under the title — who the parties are — is drawn beside the front region's header, not inside it, so a highlight there touched no clause and was offered Ask and Comment only. The front matter has been an addressable region since 28 Aug and the editor opens on it; the highlight now knows when both its ends are in the head. Across two clauses the owner's rule stands — never Edit, because merging numbered clauses renumbers an instrument — but Ask now opens the editing Copilot on the first clause instead of the main chat, so the reader stays beside the words.

**5 · ONE COPILOT.** The pencil opened a greeting; a highlight opened a card; the reader could not tell what Copilot was working on. One card now always says it: the whole clause, your words, your question, or — after the ✕ — the whole contract. In whole-contract mode Copilot is handed the whole contract, which needed the chat routes' per-turn cap (built to stop a runaway message) lifted for that one message only; it names clauses and never proposes wording, because a proposal about the whole contract has no clause to land in.

**6 · PLAIN ENGLISH IN THE BACKGROUND.** The third and fourth reports on long contracts had the same root: the edition was ONE request, kept only when every page came back whole. A single failed page — a provider hiccup, a proxy losing patience with a long request — threw away every page that had succeeded, and the next press paid for all of them again. The fix changes where things are kept, not how they are read: every clause is kept the moment it pairs, keyed by what the model was told about THAT clause (never its page key, which is only where it sat), so any later press — after a failure, after one clause changed — sends only what no kept reading answers. The reading became a job at the server so leaving the page does not cancel it and a second press joins instead of paying twice; the page asks how far it has got and draws the column filling in, with "Reading N of M" in its own heading. Two things are deliberately never kept: an answer cut short (its last entry may stop mid-sentence) and a page more than a quarter misfiled (the whole-edition rule, asked of one page). And the whole-edition cache no longer serves an edition with a hole as if it were whole, which is how a clause that failed to pair once used to stay blank for the life of the wording. The progress route lives under the contract rather than /api/ai/ because it is a question about a record, and one browser file counted every /api/ai/readings request as a press. Contracts read before this change carry no kept clauses, so the first change after it re-reads them once in full; after that only what moved is read.

**7 · THE LAW THE PAPER CHOOSES.** The line under the title read the workspace's market setting — where this company sits — and printed it as the contract's jurisdiction. It now prints the governing law HaTi read off the contract, the same field the Overview shows, and prints nothing about the law where none was read.

**WHAT THE RUN FOUND ON THE WAY** is in BUGLOG under this date: pre-existing reds in f277, plain-english-verify 10c, redline-verify 5 and notes-two-rooms-verify, the approval rule reading the wrong field, a playbook routing order that sends warehousing to the services book, and the whole-edition cache not deleted with its contract.

## A NAMED PERSON'S YES BEFORE ANYONE SIGNS (Young ruled 23 Sep 2026 — "Implement scenario 2")

The owner's words: *"Implement scenario 2 but scenario one i am not approving yet as it needs signifikant work. Implement 2 and merge to Main. Start from the latest main before coding."* Scenario 2 was drawn first — a Docs template with a picture of every screen and a plain-English note beside each — and the owner marked none of its decisions, so every one was built as that document recommended. Scenario 1 (a Review Desk for signed copies filed from outside HaTi) was not touched.

**WHAT THE PRODUCT HAD.** A person could be given an "overseer" in their drawer, behind a workspace switch that was off by default. It was one step at the end of the approval chain, keyed off the contract's OWNER, and decided by whoever pressed Approve while it was "next". Three things were wrong with it for the ask. Nobody ASKED: the step simply existed, so an approver found it or did not. Nobody was NAMED as the decider: an admin pressing Approve on the step's turn cleared it, which meant the approval could not say who had given it or of what. And it only knew about the LEAD: a colleague named to sign a contract somebody else raised was never caught.

**WHAT REPLACED IT.** The rule moved onto the person — Off | Always, who approves, who steps in when they are away, and whether it bites when the person leads, when they are named to sign, or both — and the approval became a thing somebody ASKS for. The request is its own record on the contract, stamped at the moment of asking with what it covers: the wording as text, the value, the currency, the dates, the parties and the signers. Anything in that list moving afterwards lapses it and the row says exactly what moved ("the value changed, KES 36,000,000 → KES 38,000,000"). Formatting does not move the text and a note is not the wording, so neither lapses it. An approval nobody uses for thirty days lapses too, because a yes given in spring is not a yes to sign in autumn.

**WHY ONE READING ON BOTH HOSTS.** The screen and the server must agree about whether a contract may be signed, and the history of this product is two readings of one fact disagreeing. So the reading is one file both hosts load, as the graph's filter already is: who needs an approval, what state it is in, whether a change lapsed it, who may decide it. The server reads it with the whole roster (a colleague's rule is admin-only, so a Viewer's browser cannot see it) and hands the answer down with every contract read, so the lead's own screen is right even where their browser could not have worked it out.

**THE PERSON WHO ASKED MAY NEVER ANSWER, AND NEITHER MAY THE PERSON THE RULE IS ABOUT.** An approval you grant yourself is not an approval. The approver decides; the backup decides; an admin may decide in their place but must write down why, because the record will show an admin overruling the arrangement the admins themselves set up.

**THE COUNTERPARTY NEVER LEARNS IT HAPPENED.** Their signing link is held until the approval is given, and if they press Sign on an older link the server answers with a neutral sentence ("This contract is not ready to be signed yet") rather than naming an internal step. The requests never travel: the payload is an allow-list and they are not on it. The same wall the review uses.

**A NEGOTIATION IS NEVER STOPPED BY IT.** The first draft carried the approval onto the share dialog's readiness list, which is the list a NEGOTIATION is sent from. That would have stopped the very round a refusal usually asks for — "ask them for 45 days to pay" is a message that has to go out. The approval now governs signing and nothing else: the signing link, the route's links, the internal signer's turn email. An older check (f79) caught the first repair reading the chain in a shape its stub did not supply; the reading went back to the fields that list always read, filtered to the rule steps, and f375 6e now MEASURES the list with a personal step pending, refused and lapsed.

**THE FIRST PHOTOGRAPH.** With email off in the test workspace, the internal signer's row on the signing order read EMAIL FAILED and offered "Try the email again" while the approval was still outstanding — because the server sent the turn email the moment the plan was saved, the outbox took it, and the signing order has always called an outbox notice a failure. Two fixes, both narrow: the turn email is held while the approval holds, and sent the moment it is given; the row draws no resend and no badge while held. The older fault (an outbox notice reads as a failure on every contract when email is off) is in BUGLOG, not fixed. The toast for asking also said "the email did not go" when the truth was "it is in the outbox"; the outbox now has its own sentence.

**THE PHONE.** The phone's approvals card presses the desktop's own verb, so it needed nothing new to decide — but an admin deciding in the approver's place must write a reason and the phone had nowhere to write one. The card now carries the desktop card's note box for a personal approval, required only where it is.

**WHAT IS DORMANT.** The old workspace switch left the approval-rules panel; its stored value is still read, as the default for a person whose rule was set before this and never answered, so nobody's contracts changed on the day of the deploy. `overseerFor` and `saveOverseerCfg` have no caller. A decision pressed onto the old step is deliberately not honoured — it cannot say who gave it or of what — so a contract approved under the old model is sent for approval once more. The owner is told this in the summary.

## ONE DOOR TO A STANDARD CONTRACT (Young's go on "One Door to Standards", 24 Sep 2026, every decision as recommended)

**HOW IT CAME.** The owner uploaded their SaaS agreement (a 60-page Maersk/nShift services contract with 118 headings, 595 clause numbers and 47 tables) and asked why HaTi could not load it as a template, then *"What do I do if I want to make the SaaS agreement a standard company contract?"* The honest answer took four paragraphs and named four doors, and the owner said: *"Do you see how this is very confusing?"* Then: *"Show me a render of how we build a feature in templates page for building a contract from scratch to standard contract using copilot, converting an already build template to standard contract and taking a contract that is built but you want to build it even further into a standard contract using copilot. Lets use templates tab as the only door to doing any of this."* The render was drawn ("One Door to Standards"); the owner asked *"Where do you name the contract or Store it in the respective folder?"*, the render answered it in the builder's head, and the owner said *"GO Ahead and build it"* — every one of the five open decisions as recommended.

**WHY THE SaaS AGREEMENT FAILED.** "Convert a document" handed the whole file to Copilot and asked it to write the template back out, blank by blank. A 60-page agreement is more wording than one answer can hold, so the answer was cut short and refused. "Save as template" on a contract read the wording line by line into plain text and every table fell on the floor. Pasted wording was filed as the OTHER side's paper. And "Make it ours" filed its copy under "Other". Four doors, four ways of copying one document.

**THE PRINCIPLE: HaTi COPIES, COPILOT ANSWERS SMALL QUESTIONS.** A document is copied by the readers every uploaded contract already goes through (the Word reader with its structure, the PDF reader, OCR for a scan) and cut into blocks by one copier, word for word: headings at their level, numbers as the paper prints them, every table. "No word changed" is CHECKED — the blocks joined back together must BE the markup that was read — never claimed. Copilot is then asked small, shaped questions: here are the gaps HaTi found (a bracket, a ruled line, a Word fill-in field, a company's name, an amount, a date), each with a line of context — which is a blank the next deal fills, which is a note to whoever drafts, which is standing wording? Thirty at a time, so a long document is no harder than a short one.

**THE FIVE DECISIONS, AS RECOMMENDED.** (1) "Make it ours" stays and becomes a shortcut into "From a template you have" with that HaTi template already chosen, so its copy is the copy every start makes. (2) Publishing with things still open asks ONCE, naming each open item as a door, and "Publish anyway" still goes on — a reminder, not a wall. (3) Suggested blanks arrive UNTICKED: nothing becomes a blank until a person ticks it, and the button's count follows the ticks. (4) The button is "+ New standard contract". (5) The name, the category and the value stream are not asked before the builder opens; HaTi fills them from what it knows (the document's own title, Copilot's reading of the kind, the contract's own stream) and they sit at the top of the builder as chips, each one press from the Template details box that already existed; Publish reminds if the stream is still empty.

**WHAT DRIVING IT FOUND, AND WHAT WAS REPAIRED ON THE WAY.** Each of these was only visible by pressing the thing in a browser:
- *A HaTi template offered its own blanks back.* The built-ins name their keys in camelCase (effDate, payDays, inspectDays); a template key is lower_snake_case, the server slugged the three it could not take, and the wording kept the old spelling — so three of seven blanks were "unplaced", a contract drawn from the copy would have printed three blanks nobody could fill, and the blank finder offered all seven `{{markers}}` back as "blanks to make". The key is now put in the template's shape on the marker and the field in one breath, and a `{{marker}}` is never a candidate. This fault was in the old "Make it ours" too; it became visible because the new first move lists what looks like a blank.
- *The liability clause was proposed twice.* The model said "Limitation of liability", the playbook's own open position is "Liability cap", and the fold compared NAMES — so both went on the list and both drew the library's liability clause. The fold now asks the kind the playbook reads a heading as.
- *A missing standard was listed twice.* The supply book holds a position AND a range on the liability cap: two standards, one missing clause. One reading now lists each category once, for the contract card and the publish question alike.
- *The card said "read 0" under an answer just paid for*, because the start asked the outline before the builder opened. And a refused outline promised to keep the reader's sentence and drew it nowhere; it is now in the box a press asks from again.
- *The strip grew to 35px.* With the chips in it, a restored draft's "Discard" button was squeezed until its word wrapped onto two lines. The strip now has a ladder asked of its own width — the chip keys fold first, then the draft chip, then Save's word (its tick stays, the word on its hover) — and Discard never wraps. Measured 30px at 1920, 1440, 1366, 1280, 1100, 1024 and 900.
- *A copied document read "18 sections not written yet".* A copied heading is the document's own heading, not an empty section of ours. One reading (tbSectionOwes) now answers for the foot, the placeholder, the walk and the publish question.
- *Twenty-seven names, amounts and dates vanished without a word* when Copilot labelled only some of the candidates. What is not answered is counted and said.

**WHAT IS NOT BUILT, SAID OUT LOUD.** The Template details box's "None yet" stream option does not clear a stream (it falls back to the current one) — pre-existing, logged. The server's template routes accept only the five built-in categories, so a company-added category cannot be saved onto a template — pre-existing, logged. A template written from scratch prints its first section heading as the document's title when published (the builder's paper shows the template's name above it) — pre-existing in the builder's own outline, logged. The two dialogs the one door replaced (the "New standard template" form and the Copilot conversion) are kept whole with no caller, one line from coming back, as this product keeps retired readings.

## THE PROTOTYPE'S FACES ACROSS THE PLATFORM (Young ruled 24 Sep 2026)

The owner compared HaTi with the "HaTi — Production Polish" prototype and found the type did not match: HaTi drew IBM Plex Sans on screens, JetBrains Mono (a typewriter face) on every figure and reference, and Plex again on the contract; the prototype draws Geist on screens and figures and Source Serif 4 on the paper. Asked what HaTi used, then: "change the font in HaTi to match the prototype approach across the platform."

The swap is three token edits because the fonts already flowed through four tokens. Two decisions were taken and said: IBM Plex Sans stays loaded and is named second in every stack, because Geist has no Greek and F85 exists precisely so a Greek name does not drop to a system sans; and `--font-code` keeps a real monospace, since a SHA-256 fingerprint reads as code. Source Serif 4 was served as separate files rather than inlined, because its optical-size axis makes it about a megabyte and unicode-range lets a reader fetch only what the page draws. One gap showed only on screen: the negotiate page's clause headings are h4s, which the shell dresses in its heading face, so the paper there mixed Geist headings with serif wording until `.rl-paper :is(h1…h6)` named the paper's face. The kicker above the title stayed a label in Geist, as the prototype draws it.

**HOW IT CAME.** A screenshot of the foot under the Contracts table: the VALUE STREAMS key (each stream's colour bar beside its name) on one line and "40 per page" on the line below, and the words *"delete this from both the contracts and negotiations pages."* The foot is one builder drawing both pages; on Negotiations the same spot says "one page — every group whole" instead of "40 per page", so that was put to the owner before anything moved. *"Remove it too."*

**WHY THE KEY COULD GO.** It was kept on 22 Aug with a reason written beside it: the stripe down the left edge of every row was "the thing on this page with no other explanation". That stopped being true on 21 Sep 2026, when the redesign's second pass moved the colour bar INTO the value-stream cell, beside the stream's own name. From then on the key printed the same fact a second time, and on the owner's workspace (eleven streams) it wrapped the foot into three lines — the "wall" the 22 Aug note had set out to avoid. The page size is still said where it matters: the count reads "Showing 1–40 of 50 · page 1 of 2".

**THE BOARD IS THE SAME PAGE.** The Contracts page's Board view draws the same key above its columns through `pipeBoardHtml`, which is shared with the My Queue page. The owner named two pages, so the builder gained `opts.legend` and only the Contracts page passes `false`; My Queue's markup is byte for byte what it was. The count, the pager, the board's columns and cards, and My Queue's key are CONTROLS and pass on both sides.

**THE COLOUR CENSUS.** theme-tokens-verify now reports its two register screens as changed: the Marketing violet and Manufacturing amber are gone, because on that test's three-contract book only the key ever drew them. It is an owned difference, audited as a set (two gone, nothing added) — but the baseline edit was refused by the session's permission check, so it was left alone and logged rather than forced. Every other red line in that file is red identically at the parent.

**IMAGE 1 — THE VALUE STREAM COLUMN.** Ringed on the Negotiations table: "Remove the value stream column from both pages as well but not from the filter." The Stream filter chip stays, and so does sorting by stream: the Sort dropdown already offers sorts with no column of their own (risk, title), and it offers this one too. Nothing the rows carried is lost: every dated item is a dot that opens its contract, every undated one is counted in "No clock on these" with a door onto exactly those contracts, and "See all N" opens the whole list — it used to stand down at four or fewer because the rows were then on screen, and now it is the one door, so it always draws. It answers only on the room now, the guard the negotiate page's own Escape has always had. Images 2 and 3 are undone and nothing else is.
