## DESIGN OPTIONS, AND THE PAGE CHECKLIST — TWO HABITS BORROWED FROM EMIL KOWALSKI'S SKILLS (owner-asked 24 Sep 2026)

**HOW IT CAME UP.** The owner asked what is in github.com/emilkowalski/skills — thirteen instruction packs ("skills") for AI coding assistants by Emil Kowalski (Vercel, Linear, the Sonner library), MIT licensed, mostly about animation — and then: *"could this repo help me design the faces of the pages in hati?"* The honest answer was: a little. It is about how things move and feel, not how pages look — no colour scheme, no spacing rules, no page layouts, almost nothing on tables, cards, forms and filters, which are what HaTi's pages are made of. Its taste is Apple's, Vercel's, Linear's and Raycast's, and some of it contradicts the owner's rulings outright: `apple-design` asks for translucent, blurred bars ("not opaque bars"), where HaTi's shell bar is solid brand colour by the 21 Sep ruling. And it is written for developers: its reports are Before/After tables of CSS. The recommendation was not to install it, and to borrow the two habits in it that are METHOD rather than taste. The owner: *"okay i want to borrow this"*, quoting both.

**WHY IT IS WRITTEN HERE AND NOT INSTALLED.** An installed skill brings its own orders — a fixed opening line, a required code table, its own idea of what good looks like — and they would sit beside this rulebook and pull against it. Two habits in HaTi's own words sit UNDER the rulebook instead: every option still obeys NO NEW BANDS, THE SIX QUESTIONS and the contract's pixels. Nothing was copied from the repo; the credit is for the ideas.

**WHAT WAS TAKEN FROM `prototype`, AND WHAT WAS NOT.** Taken: one part of a page per round; three options by default, five at most; each a different direction named for its idea, never "Option A/B/C"; two options that differ only in colour or wording are one option; every option finished and native to the product (its own tokens and faces), with realistic content and nothing dead to press; shown one at a time, full size, in its real surroundings, with a switcher (a button each, number and arrow keys, an instant flip) — never shrunk side by side, which misjudges spacing and size; a table naming when each option wins and what it costs; another round around a chosen one; only the chosen one built. NOT taken: building the switcher as a route inside the product and deleting it afterwards (HaTi's options are drawn as an Artifact, and nothing enters the product until the owner picks); the skill's own switcher markup (the idea is kept, nothing is copied); and its rule never to name a favourite. The owner has taken recommended answers routinely ("every decision as recommended") and did not ask to change that, and Claude's own standing instructions ask for a recommendation — so one recommendation with its reason stays, after the table, never by opening on that option or dressing it better.

**WHAT WAS TAKEN FROM `apple-design`.** Only the four questions, from its part on design foundations: hierarchy (the most important thing is the most obvious), grouping (nearness means relationship), specific labels (a label names what is behind it) and wayfinding (where am I, how do I get out). The rest of that skill — springs, glass, haptics, its type rules — is not adopted.

**HOW THE CHECKLIST SITS BESIDE THE SIX QUESTIONS.** The six are asked before anything visible is BUILT, and their answers stay quiet. The four are asked of a DESIGN — every option before it is shown, and any page the owner asks to have reviewed — and their answers are spoken: a review answers them in plain English, and a "no" on an option is fixed or named as that option's cost. The sixth question and the checklist's fourth overlap on purpose: one walks a journey, the other asks it of a single screen.

**WHAT IT CHANGES.** Until now options came as boards side by side and were answered with letters ("Image 1 = B, Image 2 = D", 17 Sep; "three formats drawn, and he picked A", 22 Sep). From now on they come one at a time at full size and are answered by name. An exact instruction is still built as given, with no round of options.

## THE MAP ON HOME — THE TILES LEFT, AND NEEDS YOUR DECISION CAME BACK WITH TWO ROWS (Young ruled 24–25 Sep 2026)

**HOW IT CAME.** The first job done under the new DESIGN OPTIONS habit. The owner asked for "an executive high level view and not too dense"; three really different directions were drawn full size on the real Home, one at a time with a switcher ("Executive Home Options"): a Briefing, a Map, and a Scorecard. The owner picked the Map by name, then asked for one change ("it is heavy on the cash side. make it so you have a toggle for review in cash or in quantity as in number of contracts"), then a second ("instead of needs your decision, delete it and replace with prepared for you"), then "Build it and merge to main".

**WHAT THE MAP IS.** One card, the page's full width: where the book stands by stage (a bar in three shades and a legend under it), what comes up for renewal over the next twelve months (a column per month, split into decision made · due · not due yet, the ninety-day window boxed, the busiest two months after the window bracketed), and three facts down the side — what could hurt you (the Exposure tab's leading row), what is owed to us, and how long agreements take to sign. Every figure is a door onto the list that makes it, and a zero draws and refuses the press. Nothing in it is a new reading: stages are the tiles' old reading, months are the renewal card's own, the facts are Insights', the obligations worklist's and the turnaround tile's.

**WHY COUNT AT REST.** The owner's complaint was that the drawing was heavy on cash. Count is the view everybody may see (money obeys the values permission, and a reader without it gets no switch at all), and it answers the question an executive asks first — how many — before how much. Value is one press away and remembered for that person in that browser.

**THE ROWS THAT WOULD HAVE BEEN LOST.** Before "Needs your decision" was deleted, every kind of row it drew was checked for another home. Signatures, approvals, reviews and renewals inside thirty days were already rows in the bell (and on Approvals & signing, and on the Map). Two were said NOWHERE else: a negotiation the other side has been waiting on past the standard, and a colleague asking to join a negotiation this reader leads. Both became registered bell kinds, off the same two sources the card read, so they reach exactly the people the card reached. The first build of the quiet-desk row dropped the card's own tag — how long it had sat — and was caught by the runway browser file when it was re-pointed; the age leads the sub-line now.

**WHAT WENT WITH THE TILES, SAID OUT LOUD.** The desktop tiles were the only door from Home onto the Insights payment-terms tab, the compliance count, the import queue and Copilot's coverage. Those readings are still counted and still offered on the phone's own tile sheet; on the desktop they are reached from their own pages. The phone's tile has only ever printed the count line, not the second line the payment-terms tile carries (the split between the two sides) — measured, recorded, not changed.

**WHAT IS KEPT AND DRAWS NOTHING.** js/runway.js (the line of time), deskCids (there is no second list on Home to evict from), rowsThatFit (its only caller was the card) and hmDashSlices' decisions reading (still the bell's renewal rows). Each stays published and tested so the next screen that wants it does not rebuild it.

**THE NETS.** One of the browser files carried a leak the new Home exposed: the section proving that a month's number matches the list it opens staged three contracts inside the renewal window and never put them back, so the overnight-desk control two sections later measured that stage instead of an empty desk. The staged fields are restored now. Ten browser files and twelve node files were re-pointed in place, each with the ruling beside it; every claim that could pass against the parent is named a control.

**THE STAGE DOOR, FOUND BY DRIVING IT.** The lifecycle tile's stage door wrote its stage into whichever seat the register was last on. The Negotiations list is the same table on its own seat, and the seat stays set when the reader leaves, so after a visit to Negotiations the door said "In review · 2" and opened a Contracts list of 4 — the fault regShowOnly and the shell's search box had each been fixed for, in a third place. The Map's stage door puts the Contracts seat back before it reads anything, and lets go of a named set left over from an earlier door. home-page-verify 6b drives it: red with the old handler, green with the new one.

The color code of the drafting, review and executed should match the color coding in the contracts list page. And below prepared for you card, add bring back the needs your attention card but only have 2 lines and nothing more."*

**A QUARTER, MEASURED BOTH SIDES.** The card was measured in a real browser before a line moved: 544.9px tall at 1280, 1366, 1440 and 1920 alike (its height is set by its own parts, not the window), and 671.4 at 1100, where the three facts stack under the charts. **TWO ROWS, AND WHAT "NOTHING MORE" LEFT OUT.** The rows are the card's own, in its own order (reviews owed, quiet desks, join requests, signatures with something before them, renewal decisions, contracts sitting in review), and exactly two are drawn on every screen — a number, not a measurement: the fitted list (hmFitDecisions, a floor of four and a ceiling of forty) is not back, and neither is the line of time. A CAP IS A FACT: the head counts the whole list and "See all" opens every contract on it. The list was lifted into one reading, hmDecisionItems, so the rows, the count in the head, the See all door and the checks that press it cannot disagree. The desk above evicts the renewals it draws from this list again, the day-old rule restored as it stood. The two bell rows added when the card left stay: the bell says everything owed to you, the card only the first two.

**TWO SMALL THINGS ON THE WAY.** A tag was escaped twice (once where the row was built and once where it was drawn); it is a plain string now and escaped once. And the empty line drew a frame of its own inside the card's frame — the rows had a rule taking that frame away and the empty line had been missed — so "Nothing to decide" reads as one line under the heading, not a box in a box (photographed before and after; f382 pins the name escaped once).


## TWO COPIES OF ONE CONTRACT — THE WORKING COPY AND THE SIGNING COPY (Young ruled 25 Sep 2026, picks 1A 2B 3A 4A 5A 6A)

*"Now i would like to Review the contract issue. When a contract goes to the document page, the negotiation page as well, it should look Like its on Microsoft Word waiting to be edited. But when you go to the signing page it should look exactly like how it was designed in standard templates or wherever it was designed and stored. Distinction between when negotiating vs when signing it. Create a design of how this would look like. No code."* A design came first ("HaTi — Working copy and signing copy", a canvas of the Document tab, the Negotiate page, the Signing tab, the last signing page and their paper), then how Plain English and X-ray would read beside it (only the left page changes; neither is drawn on the Signing tab), then *"implement the proposals and merge to main"* — built with the recommended pick on each of the six decisions: 1A pages with a gap like Word, 2B the letterhead faded to one line in the top margin, 3A no ruler and no status bar (the page number sits faded in each page's foot), 4A the signing copy's size control zooms the whole page, 5A the places to sign only on the signing copy, 6A their changed PDF signed as the agreed words on a plain page, said in the control row.

**THE ONE DESIGN DECISION EVERYTHING RESTS ON: THE SHEET STAYS ONE ELEMENT.** The obvious build — cut the document into one element per page — was refused before a line was written, because half the product walks the PAINTED page: Plain English pairs its readings against the painted headings, X-ray places its marks by containment, the sign spots anchor under a clause id, the notes' markers sit in the left gutter, the field link finds a blank by its key, a highlight is a Range. Every one of them would have had to learn pages. Instead a block that would cross from one page into the next is moved down by more `margin-top`, and a layer drawn OVER the sheet paints the grey gap between pages, the corner marks and each page's head and foot. No element is inserted into the wording and none changes parent, so every reader finds exactly what it found. The layer's words are CSS generated content (`attr()`), so no copy, Range or `textContent` ever reads "Page 1 of 6" as part of the contract.

**NOTHING IS EVER CUT.** The gap band is painted over the sheet, so anything crossing it is hidden — exactly as Word hides a changed clause's bar at a page break. Wording must therefore never cross it, and the planner guarantees that: a block is never split, a heading keeps company with the WHOLE of the block under it (a first draft kept only 44px of it and left a heading at the foot of a page over nothing, which the screenshot showed at once), and a block too tall for any page — a long table, one enormous paragraph — GROWS its page rather than lose a line. two-copies-verify asks it of every text rectangle on the paper against every gap, on all three screens.

**FOUR THINGS ONLY A REAL PAGE SHOWED.** (1) A layout that reset the sheet's padding to make the last page whole deleted the padding outright on the second pass: the sheet is written with a `padding` shorthand holding a `var()`, and such a shorthand answers `''` for its longhand, so putting the "old" value back wrote nothing — every page after a re-break lost its bottom margin. The air is `.pg-sheet::after{height:var(--pg-extra)}` now and the padding is never touched. (2) Margins COLLAPSE, so pushing a block by margin-top can move it less than asked; a correction pass measures and makes up the difference, reading every position before writing any (one layout per pass, not one per block — the first version forced a layout per block). (3) A layout asked of a HIDDEN sheet (the other copy, off-tab) measured zero and cleared pages that were still right; a sheet with no width is now left alone and re-broken when the watcher hears its width come back. (4) A clause heading drawn in a flex row beside its tag or pencil is not an `h2` itself, so it was not treated as a heading until the planner learned that a short row CARRYING a heading is one.

**THE SIGNING COPY.** A fixed 794px page (A4 at 96px to the inch; 1122.5 tall, not rounded — 1123 drifts half a pixel a page), the company's design at full strength: the letterhead on page one, a slim running head after it, the design's own footer with "Page 2 of 6" on every page (the design's footer builder is handed the number as part of its line, so it sits where the design sets its words), every field as the words filled in and an empty one as a paper form's ruled line. It is ALWAYS WHITE — the page that gets signed and printed — so the dark theme's paper and the reader's text size stop at its edge (light tokens pinned on `.pg-sheet.pg-sign`, `--doc-scale:1`). The size control is 4A: the page is laid out once and the whole of it is scaled, so the pages you read are the pages you sign; "fit" is the default, the reader's choice is kept per browser. Two-column designs show ONE column on the signing pages for now — a page-maker that moves whole blocks cannot fill two columns a page at a time, and a column running the whole length of a long contract is not a page anybody signs — said to the owner.

**THE PLACES TO SIGN, ON THE PAGE (5A).** The parties' lines become the boxes a signature goes in, the reader's own in the accent with a "Sign here" tab pointing at it from the margin, every other party's in grey. The tab points in from the NEAREST margin, read off the layout, because the first version pointed at the second party's box across the first party's. Only on the signing copy: the working copy keeps plain ruled lines, and a spot placed on the record is not drawn there (two-copies-verify 5a places one and looks).

**THEIR PAPER (6A).** Three answers, and our letterhead on none of them. A PDF or a scan nobody changed a word of is signed as their file itself, every page as they sent it, with a signature page added after it — HaTi cannot mark a place inside a PDF's own pages, so the places are on a page of their own, which says so and carries no page number (it is not "Page 1 of 1" of anything, which the first version said). A Word file is set in its OWN look, read off the file when it is read (`report.layout`): its page size, its margins, its face (named through the theme where the file names it that way), its size, its header and its footer, with a page-number field and the words that framed it ("Page … of …") taken out so the signing copy numbers its own. NOTHING IS GUESSED — a value the file does not state is absent and the A4 default stands in. The face first failed to reach the wording because every rule on the sheet reads `var(--font-doc)` and `var(--doc-scale)`; the page sets those two tokens rather than a `font-family`. Their PDF with changed words is 6A: the agreed words on a plain page, and the control row says "rebuilt from their file with the agreed words".

**PRINT.** A printer paginates on its own and truncates a margin at a page break, so the long sheet cannot simply be printed. `pagesPrintPages` rebuilds each screen page as a box of its own holding copies of exactly the blocks the screen put there, each inside a shallow copy of the containers it sat in (a container that began on an earlier page does not open again), the screen's border taken off and the box narrowed by exactly that much so not one line wraps differently, with the same furniture from the same builder. A temporary `@page{size:A4;margin:0}` is added for the print and removed on `afterprint`, so every other print is as it was. Measured: Export PDF produced three A4 pages matching the screen.

**REFUSAL 3.** Measured on MK-A2 at 1440 wide, parent → now: the Document tab 271.9 → 271.9 (with a design, 352.1 → 272.9 — the letterhead left the flow for the top margin); the Negotiate page 286.7 → 286.7 (and 289.7 → 289.7 with a design); **the Signing tab 271.9 → 301.9** (design 352.1 → 382.1). The thirty pixels are the signing page's own 64px top margin against the working copy's 34px — both sheets start at the same pixel, so no chrome grew — and the approved design drew the signing page with that margin. The standing rule says a growth in that number needs the owner's yes, so it is said to the owner rather than assumed. signing-on-paper-verify 1c asserted the two tabs identical (ONE SHEET, TWO TABS, 29 Aug) and is re-pointed in place to the relation the new ruling keeps.

**NOT BUILT, said out loud**: the clause editor's canvas is not paged (it is one clause on a page of its own); the phone and the read-only view link are unchanged; two-column designs are one column on the signing pages; the PDF export of their paper as it came is unchanged; places to sign inside a PDF's own pages cannot be marked. PRE-EXISTING and left red: signing-on-paper-verify 4a and the journey after it fail identically at the parent — the signature pad refuses Adopt & sign until its intent line is ticked (13 Sep) and the file never ticks it.

**THE CHECKS THIS RULING REVERSED, AND THE ONES IT ONLY MOVED.** Two claims said the Negotiate page's paper was flat and warm — F89 (2) in node and redline-verify 2 in a browser, both from the 22 Aug render, where a sheet filling its column had "nothing to float above" and a cream tint was what made paper read as paper beside a white card. The owner's new picture reverses both halves: the working copy is WHITE and lies on the desk like a page in Word, and what makes it read as paper is what a page in Word has — its edge, its shadow and the grey between one page and the next. Both claims now assert the working copy's own three tokens, so the Document tab and the Negotiate page cannot disagree about a page. redline-verify 2b's "gaps between clauses are even and tight" measured one gap of 160px the first time the paper was paged: the distance across a page break (a page's foot, the grey, the next page's head) is not a gap between two clauses, and the check now reads which page each clause sits on off the page-maker's own record rather than guessing from a size. Three more were only MOVED: signing-on-paper-verify 1c (above), f225's region slice (it ran from the grid to the canvas, and the canvas now lives in the one builder per copy far above the room's template — anchored on the canvas, the slice ran backwards and read nothing) and f278 (1), which counts the scroll listeners in the room and names each: the signing copy's "Page 2 of 6" follows the reader's scroll, a third listener that folds nothing. And one piece of order: the Word reader's new names were first put at the FRONT of its publish lists, and f366 pins the list opening `{docxStyledIsWording,` — they sit at the end now.

## THE COMPACT BUTTON LADDER (Young picked it 26 Sep 2026, off the "HaTi Button Audit" page)

*"I am concerned that the buttons in Hati seem disproportionate. Review again platforms like SAP, Apple, and other best in class SaaS platforms and advise. Also review the uniformity of the buttons and how we can along them to seem aligned across Hati. No coding."* The review (the private page "HaTi Button Audit") measured 250 pressable controls on 28 screens and dialogs: bordered and filled buttons at eleven heights from 22 to 48, three label weights, four text sizes, four corner shapes, text boxes at 28 to 36 beside buttons at 30, emoji and typed arrows standing in for icons, and dialogs whose buttons scrolled out of view. It drew three options — Compact, Standard, Comfortable — on real screens, with ten alignment rules that hold for all three. The owner picked Compact: *"Implement compact and merge to main. Going to bed now so work autonomously."* The touch step-up for the iPad was a separate yes or no and was not chosen, so it was not built.

**THE LADDER, SAID ONCE.** Three rungs in `:root` — `--ctl-h-sm` 22, `--ctl-h` 28, `--ctl-h-lg` 32 — with the side padding (8 · 10 · 12), the icon sizes (14 · 14 · 16), the gap from icon to word (6) and between buttons (8) beside them. `.ui-btn` reads the everyday rung, `.ui-btn-sm` the row rung at 12px, `.ui-btn-lg` the large rung. **`.ui-btn-lg` CHANGED MEANING**: since 10 Sep it had meant "a head-row button" — the base height at weight 400, worn by eight head-row buttons so they read quieter than everything else. With one label weight for every button that difference is exactly what the review called disproportionate ("the same Share button is medium weight in the contract room and regular on the Negotiate page"), so those eight wear the base `.ui-btn` and the name now says what it is: the one large act of an area (the Sign button, a first password, an empty page's invitation), always the filled one. f385 asks that relation of every place it is used.

**A TEXT BOX IS THE BUTTON'S HEIGHT.** `--field-h` is `var(--ctl-h)`, a reference and never a second number, and a one-line box takes it as its HEIGHT rather than a floor — a floor let a box grow past the button beside it, which is rule 2's whole complaint. The shared field styles (HATI_FLD, RV_FLD, WZ_ST) read it; the forms still written in the older utility classes got `.ui-fld`; the signing-order editor's row boxes (32–33px) and the obligation form's amount box (a currency in front of a number, 36px) were found by opening the dialogs and measuring every box, and moved onto it.

**ONE LABEL WEIGHT.** Every button label is 500; the filled face says which act leads, never the weight (Apple: "use style — not size"). A switch sitting in a row of buttons reads its resting halves at 500 too and keeps the lit half bold — the 11 Sep ruling "only the shaded one is bold" is kept, and the row reads at one weight, which is what that ruling was for. The redline row's Accept used to lead by its 700; it leads now by coming first and being the only verb in the full accent ink. Tabs keep their own rule.

**THE ROW RUNG IS 22 DRAWN AND 24 TO PRESS, AND THE FIRST ATTEMPT WAS WRONG.** WCAG 2.5.8 asks for a 24 × 24 target; SAP draws its touch buttons 36 inside a 44 pressable area. `.ui-btn-sm::after` is an invisible edge that moves no layout. It was written `inset:-1px` and the browser check found it adding nothing: an absolutely placed box is placed against its parent's PADDING box, which sits 1px inside the border, so -1px reached exactly the border's edge and a real press half a pixel under a row's menu landed on the cell behind it. It is -2px now, and both f385 and compact-ladder-verify measure it (the node file does the border arithmetic; the browser file presses half a pixel outside the drawn box, above and below).

**TEXT BUTTONS HAVE ONE LOOK.** `.ui-link`: the accent, 500, no underline, at least `--tap-min` tall, a drawn arrow where one is needed; `.ui-link-danger` for a text button that throws something away (Revoke a link or a session, Remove key). The review named three ("Run →", "See all", "show a flat list", 17 to 21px tall). A sweep of every hand-styled `<button>` with its own font size and no border then found about forty-five more — share-link rows, the risk scan's Go to wording and Dismiss, the counterparty page's toggles, Settings' Reset to defaults, Insights' Regenerate, Show all and Read them — and moved each that is a verb standing on its own. What stayed, on purpose: a link inside a sentence keeps its underline (reg-flat, the import manifest's "template", "Use this" in the work-shape line, the metadata check's "Use …", the library's fix links); tabs; menu rows; a contract's own name as the door onto it; the dormant email-setup line, which nothing draws.

**ONE FILLED BUTTON PER AREA.** "In repeated rows the main act can take the accent colour, never the fill." `.ui-btn-accent` is the ink without the fill, written after the redesign's white face and one class heavier so source order cannot beat it (the same reason `.ui-btn-danger` sits there). The rows that still filled every row were found by reading every `ui-btn-primary` inside a `.map(` and pressed into the accent: the desk's join requests, the import queue, and the playbook review window, whose cards each carried a filled lead and made one dialog hold ten filled buttons.

**DRAWN ICONS ONLY.** No emoji and no typed arrows, carets, crosses, ticks or plus signs inside a button's words. The dozen the review listed were replaced first; the sweep f385 now runs over every `<button>` in the desktop product found about a dozen more (the cohort act's caret, the wizard's "← templates", the approval rules' "↗", the X-ray's Obligations door, the friction brief's "✕ Clear" and "open →", the negotiation room's "← Doc", the needs-you chip's arrow, three dictionary labels carrying ▾ or ✕, and the writing bar's two carets). `plusLed(html)` turns a label's leading "+ " into the drawn plus. ICONS gained chevU, chevL, more (three dots, for every "⋯") and refresh. The writing bar's caret is `RICH_BAR_CARET`, deliberately kept out of RICH_BAR_ICON: that set is the bar's nine tools, all authored 15 wide so one rule scales them by exactly 1.2 (f266 pins the premise, and caught the first draft). Named and kept: Reports (off the rail, kept byte-identical by the redesign), the signature pad's "★ Saved" tab (a tab, and the pad is the counterparty's too), the wizard's dormant streams picker.

**A DIALOG'S BUTTONS STAY IN VIEW.** "Dialog footer: right side, Cancel then the main act. Always the same order, always in view while the body scrolls." A static read of every Cancel found none standing after its dialog's main act — the order was already right almost everywhere, as the review had said. What was missing was the second half. Ninety dialogs each build their own foot, so rather than editing ninety builders the foot is FOUND: `dlgFootOf(panel)` takes the last row in the panel that holds a ladder button and nothing but buttons (an empty spacer allowed) with nothing readable after it, and `dlgPinFoot(panel)` marks it `data-dlg-foot` so the sheet pins it to the panel's bottom edge. It is armed by openModal — the one door every dialog comes through — and released by closeModal beside the focus trap and the drag; a MutationObserver re-finds it when a dialog steps without opening again. Sticky acts only once the panel scrolls, so a dialog that fits looks exactly as it did, and `data-scrolls` on the panel is what draws the hairline above a pinned foot. A dialog that names its own `.dlg-foot` (the Send dialog) is left alone. Measured by opening a dozen dialogs in a 1280 × 460 window: in every one that ends in a row of buttons the row was found, Cancel came first and every button was inside the panel without scrolling (the New standard chooser's first screen ends in tiles, not a row of buttons, and is left as it is).

**REFUSAL 3.** The first line of the agreement, measured on the same stage at the parent and after, at 1440 × 900: the Document tab 271.9, the Negotiate page 286.7, the Signing tab 301.9 — unmoved to the tenth of a pixel. The rows above the paper keep their own heights, so shorter buttons inside them move nothing.

**THE CHECKS.** f385 pins what the stylesheet says (23 claims; 21 red at the parent, the other two named walls). compact-ladder-verify measures what a reader sees on the real pages — the Contracts page, the room's head, the Document tab, the Signing tab, the Negotiate page, a dialog in a short and a tall window, the New agreement pop-up, and a glyph sweep over every page it visits (29 checks, 21 red at the parent; it prints 30px everywhere, a 48px Sign at weight 600, the Negotiate row's verbs at 24/600, 34–36px boxes and an 18px Cancel in the New agreement pop-up, and "Run →" typed on every checks row). Re-pointed in place, each with its reason: f89 (Accept leads by its ink, not its weight), f91 (Draft new agreement is the base `.ui-btn`), f240 and f245 (the label weight and the rung), f265 (an ORDER asked as an order, not two adjacent lines), f277 (11) (the head row's rung is the base button now), f305 (the door's words read with the drawn arrow taken out), f306 (9) (➤ is a drawn send), f313 (39) (the gap asked as the relation to the acts row), f314 (4) (the playbook review's lead wears the accent), f345 (4) (the field token is the rung, taken as height), f368 (5) (the list cap re-derived: the foot 55 → 53, the Import row 28 → 35).

**THE BROWSER SET, BOTH VERSIONS, CHECK BY CHECK.** The whole browser set ran on the branch, and every file that failed there was run again on the unmodified parent in a separate worktree, its failing checks compared by name. Six files failed on the branch for a reason that was this ladder's own, and each was re-pointed in place to the relation it always meant: counterparty-leads-verify 3d and one-door-verify 1a / templates-tabs-verify 9a typed a number or a character the ladder changed (a 32px box, a typed "+"), and read the box height live and the drawn plus now; flat-rows-and-alerts-verify 3c and pages-read-alike-verify 5 measured "not bold" as "at most 400", the row's weight that day, and ask one weight across the row that is not a bold one; nego-redesign-verify 13 pinned a hand-set 18px glyph and asks the rung's own icon size. Every other failing file failed the same checks on both versions — four of them (counterparty-reading-and-more, keeps-your-place, reopen-a-refusal, six-round-audit) stop on the same driver error at the same line on both, so they were compared by hand.

**THE COLOUR CENSUS, UNCUT.** The census prints at most four colours a side, so it was run on both versions with that cut lifted (the test's own source compiled in memory, nothing written to either checkout) and the whole set difference compared screen by screen. It is exactly two moves, both deliberate: the approval card's Reject button left Tailwind's rose (#E11D48 ink, #FECDD3 edge) for the ruby tokens every other destructive button wears (`--st-ruby-line` #ECBAB5 arrives), on the five contract-room screens in the light theme; and a HELD Sign button lost its pale accent wash (`bg-brand-100`, accent-500 at 16% in the dark theme) because a held act wears the secondary face and never the fill. The second is the only difference on menu--dark, which is why that one screen goes from green to red. The baseline was NOT re-recorded: it is already red on nineteen screens at the parent for reasons that are not this change, and re-recording would absorb them. Listed in BUGLOG.

## ONE BUTTON: ONE LINE, ONE SIZE PER ROW, ONE LIGHT EDGE (Young ruled 26 Sep 2026, three screenshots)

*"I still see a lot of inconsitencies. image 1, buttons should never wrap text. Image two, the buttons should be the same size and likely the size of the needs your decision card. Image 3, some buttons have dark outlines when the common approach is a light grey outline. Put these in a work job to be fixed."* The work order (WORKORDER-button-consistency.md) measured each on the merged tree before a line moved; then, the next morning, *"fix the three button issues first. Start from the latest main."*

**THE WRAP WAS A RULE NOBODY WROTE.** On the Approvals & signing page, "Open the gate" broke onto two lines (88 × 31) once long contract titles squeezed its column to 116px, and "Value ≥ SEK 5M" broke beside it while the Value column was clipped. No family said anything about wrapping, so every button inherited `white-space:normal` from the page, and no column that held a button had a floor. A sweep of every page, the room's tabs, the Negotiate page and the main dialogs listed the families that draw a LABELLED button — short words, nothing block-level inside — and ONE `:is(...)` rule now says `nowrap` for all nineteen. **Every entry is one class on purpose**: `:is()` takes the weight of its heaviest argument, so a single id or a two-class selector in that list would silently lift every family above the rules that dress it, which is a cascade fight nobody would ever see in the source. The comment above the everyday button that promised "a two-line label still grows" said the opposite of the rule and was taken out. The Contracts row menu's cell measured 28px of column at a 1024 window against a 22px square plus two ordinary paddings, so the menu button was cut; the cell takes less side padding now.

**HOME'S DESK VERBS WERE A FAMILY THE LADDER MISSED.** Prepared for you drew its verbs at 28px, 13px, weight 600 and FILLED on every row, beside Needs your decision's 22px row verbs twelve pixels below — a hand-sized family written before the Compact ladder, which the ladder's sweep had not reached because it carried its own class. `hmRowBtnCls(cls)` is the one reading both of Home's rows ask (the desk, and the dormant triage row, so a second card cannot bring the old size back): the ladder's row rung, the lead act in the accent's INK rather than a fill on every row (one filled button per area), and Put away as the ladder's text button. `.hm-tri-b` stays as a hook and states no box of its own; the act row stops stretching its buttons to its tallest item.

**THREE OUTLINE COLOURS IN ONE ROW, READ OFF THE OWNER'S OWN PIXELS.** The Document tab's control row painted navy round the view switch, #CBD3D0 round Export and Open Negotiate, and #E2E7E5 round the text-size stepper. `--btn-edge` was `--rule-strong`, the darker grey, and three families named their own edge rather than the token. It is `--color-divider` — the stepper's own #E2E7E5 — by day and stays `--rule-strong` at night, where the lighter one would disappear on the dark ground; each value is said once. Every family that named its own edge reads the token now, the seams between switch halves included. Three things were deliberately NOT lightened: a switch still fills its lit half (the fill is what says which is on), a text box keeps its stronger `--field-line` (a lighter one would stop telling a reader where to type), and a filled button's edge is its own fill.

**THE CHECKS.** f386 pins what the stylesheets say (14 claims; 9 red at the parent that wrote the work order; the walls and controls pass on both). button-consistency-verify measures what only a rendered page knows — a label on one line under long titles, the edge each control really paints, the two cards' verbs side by side (17 checks, 11 red at the parent). f335 (5) and f364 (9) had pinned the old token's NAME on a pair of controls; they ask the relation they meant — the pair shares one edge token.

## THE LIST INSPECTOR — CONTRACTS, NEGOTIATIONS, APPROVALS & SIGNING (Young picked it 26 Sep 2026, option 3 of "Contract List Options")

*"Prior to fixing these, I first need you to give me examples of how we can improve the design for the contracts and negotiations contract lists design. They pages do not look clean and professonal grade. No coding yet."* Three options were drawn full size beside today's two pages, photographed on the same sample book, following the design-options habit (the private page "Contract List Options"): Ledger (one calm line per contract, the table's tools on the table), Worklist (grouped by the next step), Inspector (the list with a facts panel beside it). Ledger was recommended. The owner: *"Build Inspector and apply to the approvals and signing pages as well, fix the three button issues first. Start from the latest main."*

**THE SHAPE.** A narrower list beside one contract's facts. A press on a row SELECTS it and the panel follows; opening takes a second press — the panel's own button, Enter, or a double-click — and the arrow keys move the selection. That reverses, on these three pages and only above a measured width, the old rule that one press on a row opens the contract; below the width each page keeps its full table and one press still opens, and the browser file holds both as named controls.

**ONE PANEL, THREE PAGES.** `js/views/inspector.js` draws the panel for all three; each page hands it the contract, the order of its sections and its own verbs. The head says the reference and kind, the counterparty (with "+N" where more parties are on the paper), the agreement, the status and whose move it is, then the page's acts and a ⋯. The sections are On the table, the facts, What Copilot read, and Latest; the Approvals page adds its own section first. The listener is bound once per ELEMENT and reads what to do off the element at press time — a listener that captured a contract would act on the one that was selected when it was bound.

**THE WIDTH WAS FOUND BY MEASURING.** The first line was 940 of page width. At 940 the filter row wrapped and the counterparty column was cut to 150px, so the line is 1040 — the narrowest page that holds a reference, a counterparty, a stage and a value side by side AND keeps the filter row on one line; on a laptop with the floating rail that is any window from about 1104 wide. At 1024 the list's older 760px minimum width pushed the Value column out of the card; the inspector's table is exempt from it. At the narrowest widths the Sort chip gives way first. The page records its shape so a resize that crosses the line repaints it.

**EVERY FACT IS BORROWED.** The value is the contract's own currency and only for a reader who may see money; the move is `negoMoveSay`'s; On the table reads `c.changes` raw (reading must not write — nothing here calls a function that would create a negotiation) with the other side's asks first and a count past five, and says an ask has waited past the desk's standard through the desk's own working-day walk, which the desk now publishes rather than having a second copy written here. What Copilot read is the Overview's own table: its builder was split into a reading (`ktReadingsRows`) and a drawing, so the panel and the Overview read one place. **Latest is the one fact that is not on the light list** — the list strips the trail — so the panel fetches the record once, repaints only that section and only if the same contract is still shown (a reader who arrowed on is not thrown back), and says so if the fetch fails rather than showing an empty "Latest".

**ONE DOOR ONTO EVERY ACT.** The panel's buttons are the page's own. On Contracts, Open contract leads and Open negotiation is drawn only where a negotiation has started and may be opened; on Negotiations the other way round. **"Started" was first read as "a negotiation object exists"**, and the night screenshot showed "Open negotiation" on a contract that had only been opened — opening a contract can leave an empty negotiation on the record. The Document tab has always answered that question with "a change is on it" ("Start negotiating" otherwise), so the panel asks exactly that now; two doors onto one question may not give two answers (f387 2k, red at its own parent). The ⋯ is the row's own menu, from one table of row acts that the row and the panel both press, and one function answers what "open" means for a press, Enter and a double-click. On Approvals & signing the lead act is that page's own door onto the Signing tab, and its section is the approval rule, who it waits on, who asked and how long — or, on the Signatures tab, what stands before signing, borrowed from the Signing tab's own list, three then a count. That page still decides nothing: approving, refusing and signing are not called from it.

**THE DRAWING'S FLOOR, ON BOTH SHAPES.** The options page listed what all three designs fix, and each is built in both the inspector and the full table: a name prints "&" (the contract's title reading already escapes it and the row escaped it a second time — noticed in the bug log on 25 Sep); "Non-monetary" in place of "n/m"; days left only inside 90 days; plain column names, with a sort arrow only on the sorted column; the resting reference in the quiet ink (only the selected one wears the accent, so the accent means "this one"); the head says "29 live" — it always counted the book less the declined contract, and said "29 agreements" over an All tab reading 30, which read as a disagreement; a quick view with nothing in it prints no count; a group with no rows is not drawn; the Negotiations page carries its own facts and none of the Contracts page's quick views. Table · Board, the row density and the amendment fold moved into one Display menu, so the Contracts page carries one filled button (at the parent three were filled: Draft new agreement, Table and Compact).

**WHAT THE DRAWING REVERSED, SAID OUT LOUD.** Three older rulings about these pages give way to the drawing the owner picked, on both shapes, because it is one page with two column sets. The white band of 24–25 Aug ("make it one card") is gone: the title, its facts line and the views sit on the page ground, and the filter row is the top row of the list's own white card — the band's point survives, since the filters and the rows they narrow are still one card with no seam, and the browser checks that measured the band now measure that card. The column headings are the label rung in plain words (12px, medium) rather than the redesign's bold micro caps, and a group's name keeps its strong weight over a lighter count — both read straight off the drawing's own stylesheet. And the Negotiations page's third column (whose move) takes the Contracts page's stage width, so the three columns the two pages share are cut identically in pixels, which the full tables have kept since 21 Sep; the first build had the two third columns 32px apart and the counterparty column followed.

**FOUR THINGS THE CHECKS CAUGHT ON THE WAY.** f218 caught a panel fallback that printed one contract's value in the workspace currency — removed; a contract states its own currency. f240 caught "Non-monetary" set smaller than the row it sits in. f148 caught a Swedish word copied from English ("Ref" → "Referens"). And the Swedish Stage column said "Fas" while the chip beside it said "Steg"; both say "Steg".

**THE PROBE THAT MEASURED ITSELF.** inspector-verify's first run failed "the filter row is one line" at every width in both languages. Measured: every chip sat at one top. The check counted distinct TOPS, and the row's spacer is a box with a width and no height, centred on the line — so it read as a second line. It counts the centres of boxes that have a height now. A probe's own sentinel is not data.

**NOT BUILT, said out loud.** The drawing's Owner filter on Negotiations (that page keeps the filters it has) and its Draft new agreement button on the Negotiations head; the phone.

**THE BROWSER SET, BOTH VERSIONS, CHECK BY CHECK.** The whole set ran on the branch (54 of 150 files red), and each of the 54 ran again on main's code in a separate worktree, compared by check name. Thirteen differed from main: twelve had a failing check only here, and row-density stopped on a press it could no longer make (its density buttons had moved into Display). One of the twelve (clause-editor-verify 33h, a real mouse landing a caret) passed 290 of 290 run alone and is timing under four browsers at once. The other twelve were this work's own, and none was a product fault: most measured the full table at a window where the page now draws the Inspector, and they stage the full table with the page's own stage door (`insForce(false)`), said beside the line, because every narrower window still draws it; the rest asked a relation the new shape changed the spelling of — heading words that became plain words (pair by the column's key instead), a line counter that read the card's padding as a second line, density buttons that now sit inside Display, a row that selects before it opens, a chip that lost its funnel mark, the resting chip edge fix 3 made light, and the white band the drawing reversed (asked now of the list's own card). flat-rows measures both shapes, under the old names for the full table so the known 12px date-cell exception stays in view rather than vanishing because the default shape has no date column. Fix 3: calendar and templates (light) lose #CBD3D0, the old darker edge; the Document tab, Negotiate and Signing (dark) lose the text-size stepper's own night edge; Home, the Document tab and Signing (light and dark) lose the view switch's 45% accent seam, now the same grey as its edge.
