### EVERY PARTY BUT OURS ON THE PANEL (Young ruled 26 Sep 2026)

**THE REPORT.** The same evening the four-page Inspector build was merged, the owner wrote: *"For contracts that have multiple parties, all the parties apart from the owner should be listed on the right panels. MK-430 as an example has another party in the contract as well but they are not listed on the right panels."*

**WHAT THE PANEL DID.** The list Inspector's head was built on 26 Sep with the multi-party build's own compact reading, `partiesLead`: the first outside party's name, then "+1" in a small grey box, and every other name joined on the heading's hover. That mark was designed for a ROW, where a column is a few hundred pixels wide and the multi-party build's rule was "drawn only where partiesMulti". On the panel — the one screen whose job is to say what a contract is — it meant a guarantor, a second customer or a third signatory never reached the page a reader was looking at. MEASURED at the parent on a staged three-party contract: the heading read "SAP East Africa+1" on Contracts, Negotiations and Approvals & signing alike, and the departures panel under Our standards printed the customer alone, with no mark at all.

**THE READING IS THE PARTIES MODULE'S OWN.** `insParties(c)` asks `partiesTheirs(c)` — the list every "which party" control in the product offers, which never holds our own side — and asks it only where `partiesMulti(c)`. That second condition is the multi-party build's standing rule, and here it is what keeps an ordinary two-party contract's head byte for byte what it was: f391 (2a) compares the markup whole. A reading that listed every contract's single counterparty in the new shape would have moved every panel in the product to fix one kind of contract.

**THE DRAWING.** One line per party, the name keeping the heading's own size and its own cut (`.ins-cp-n`, so a long legal name elides rather than wraps the panel), and the word the paper calls that party beside it in the quiet ink where one is recorded — "Customer", "Guarantor". The whole `partyLine` rides each line's hover. No cap: a contract holds at most PARTY_MAX parties and the panel scrolls, and a list that stopped at two would be the same silence in a new place. The heading stops being a flex row and becomes a column (`.ins-cp.is-many`). The same lines sit under the contract's name on Our standards' departures panel, where they take that line's own quiet size — that panel describes a contract too, and a reader moving between the two panels should not find a party on one and not the other.

**WHAT WAS DELIBERATELY LEFT.** The list ROWS keep their "+1": a row is a compact reading by design and the owner asked about the panels. The obligation panels say "We owe X this" / "X owes us this", and the contract panel's "On the table" section says "from X" and "sent to X"; each of those names ONE party because an obligation and a proposed change record no party at all — only a DECISION carries a party (`respPartyId`). Printing every party there would be a claim the record does not hold, so they are logged, not swept.

**WHAT WAS MEASURED.** f391 pins what the code says (14 claims; 12 red at the parent, the control 2a and the wall 2d passing on both). every-party-verify drives the real app at 1440: three contracts are given a customer and a guarantor through `partiesSet` (one with the other side's ask filed through the funnel so it is on Negotiations, the first on Approvals & signing, one that departs from a standard off HaTi's own rule-based check), and every panel is measured for two painted lines, one below the other, inside the panel, with the role beside each name and our own side absent — then again after a page refresh, which proves the parties ride the light list the server sends (HEAVY does not strip them), and the role word's contrast by day (5.82:1) and at night (7.45:1). 16 checks; 10 red at the parent.

## REDLINE HERE, SIGN THERE — A FILE THEY SIGN (Young's go, 26 Sep 2026, every decision as recommended)

*"i want to design a process in hati where by I upload a contract simply for redlining but using the same exact features and tools I have in hati now but in the end, the goal is negotiate / redline and once you are aligned with the counterparty, the process in hati ends and the counterparty takes over the process using their ways of working. At this stage i would just be waiting to sign the contract either by hand or docusign or other esign process then upload the contract back to Hati at which point the contract gets its contract number and is stored."* The owner corrected the first design: *"When we handover the contract we hand it over in microsoft word so they can redsign the document to fit how they design their local contracts. … Our aim is to simply ensure we are aligned on the wording of the contract and what they do there after is up to them."* A process map was drawn without looking at the page, the page was audited against it (fifteen gaps), the screens were corrected, and nine decisions were put with a recommendation each (the page "Redline Here, Sign There"). Then: *"go as recommended. Start from the lastest main."*

**THE NINE, AS BUILT.** (1) The contract number is given when the signed copy is FILED, not at upload. (2) A working file is listed on Negotiations only; a search on Contracts still finds it and the row says where it lives. (3) The upload asks who runs the signing, and an admin chooses which answer is ticked by default (`signRouteDefault`; "we sign in HaTi" at rest, so nothing changes on the day of the deploy). (4) They agree either through Ready to sign on HaTi's link or by our lead's "confirmed by email" tick with the day. (5) Our signatory is asked but may be skipped, and the window says what skipping costs. (6) The check before we sign is OFFERED to our signatory and recorded — never a gate, because the signature happens where HaTi cannot hold it. (7) A signed copy whose words differ is accepted only by the approver or an admin, with a reason. (8) A reminder on the fifth working day, then weekly; "is this still live?" at 60 days. (9) The signed copy comes in through the Signing tab AND through the ordinary Upload button — never through their link.

**THE ONE DESIGN DECISION EVERYTHING RESTS ON: THE ID IS THE KEY FOREVER.** The obvious build — rename RL-012 to MK-231 when it is filed — was refused before a line was written. The id is in every share token's row, every URL and deep link, every `data-*` attribute, every reminder's dedupe key, the files table, the clause locks, the audit trail, the phone's bookmarks and a reader's own localStorage keys; renaming it at filing would have orphaned all of them at the one moment the record matters most. So the number is a SECOND NAME, `c.contractNo`, and `contractRef(c)` (js/outside.js, both hosts) is the one printer: the number where there is one, else the id. A record on file has no number, so it prints exactly what it printed yesterday — byte for byte. About 150 print sites were swept across 24 browser files and the server, every one guarded `window.contractRef ? contractRef(c) : c.id`, because the modules load apart and a test world may not carry this one. What was NOT swept is as deliberate: lookups, API paths, data attributes and dedupe keys stay on `c.id`.

**THE NUMBER IS THE SERVER'S TO GIVE.** From the same counter every MK id comes from, in the very save that files the copy (asked as a DIFFERENCE on the stored record), never one a record already answers to as an id or as a number, and never moved afterwards (`contract_no` column; EXECUTED_IMMUTABLE). Working ids come off their own counter (`rlUid`); a new contract whose id is somebody's number is refused. `contractRefMatches` finds a file by either name — the deep link, the palette, the register search, and Copilot (`aiContractByRef` in the browser, `copilotGetJson` by `contract_no` on the server) — because a reader holding last month's email types the RL reference and a reader holding the signed copy types the MK one.

**THE HANDOVER IS A ROUTE, NOT A SAVE.** A save carries whatever the browser happens to hold; a handover sends a file to another company, locks the words and starts a clock. So `POST /api/contracts/:id/handover` owns it — hand · send · chase · check · partial · sendback · live · reopen · filed — writing on the STORED record, and the ordinary PUT keeps the stored `handover`, `handoverHistory` and `contractNo` (the clause locks' own rule, borrowed). `hand` asks everything again that the Signing tab asked — the route, who may lead, the negotiation settled, the approval chain, a named person's approval, the check before signing — because THE SERVER IS THE WALL. It READS the Word file it is handed (`tplZipEntry`) and refuses one with a blank left in the agreed words (`outsideBlanksIn`: "[insert …]", a bracketed capital placeholder, a `{{field}}`; "[reserved]", "[signature]" and their cousins are not blanks). It mails the file to each address and records every one.

**ONE LIST, AND IT IS THE SIGN BUTTON'S.** The Signing tab of a file they sign draws `signBlockers` — the list the Sign button has always read — with the rows that cannot apply dropped (the turn, the signers, the places to sign) and two added: our signatory (`ho-signatory`, never holds — decision 5) and a blank in the agreed words (`ho-blanks`, holds). The cap and the folder rows ask about OUR SIGNATORY rather than the reader. A second list would have been a second door, and this codebase's most expensive fault class is two screens disagreeing about what the product does.

**THE WAIT.** "With them for signature" is an overlay on the status (`HANDOVER_META`), steel, because nothing is owed by us until a reminder day. The clock is `ohWorkdays`, which is `saWorkdays` — the sign-approval reminders' own count, pinned EQUAL across a weekend and the Christmas week by f388 (2a), because two working-day counters in one product drift. The reminder is `HANDOVER_REMIND_WORKDAYS` (5), then weekly; the "still live?" question is `HANDOVER_LIVE_DAYS` (60). While it is out: the words are frozen (`HANDOVER_FROZEN`), the route is locked, HaTi takes no signature and issues no signing link, no round can start, their link READS ONLY and serves the file, and approvals do not lapse (the words cannot move under them). Reopen withdraws it and their link says so.

**THE WORD CHECK IS ABOUT WORDS.** They will redesign the file, renumber it and move the parties' block; none of that is a change. `outsideCompare` walks the agreed version's paragraphs against the signed copy's text stream: a shingle index of 1–4 word keys, an exact pass, then an LCS pass; a same-line addition IS a change; inserted text is told from text around it; a renamed defined term is named as one; a copy covering under a fifth of the agreed words is "not this agreement", and a copy read by OCR says it cannot be trusted word for word. **TWO THINGS ONLY A REAL FILE SHOWED**: the document's TITLE carried their company's name in front of the agreed title and was flagged as a changed line — the first paragraph with no marker is now allowed its company; and a short line of five or six words was looked up by its whole length rather than its first four, so it was never found at all (`a.slice(0, Math.min(4, m))`).

**WHO SIGNED.** `outsideReadCopy` reads names and dates near the signature cues. Where the signing plan names nobody for their side — the ordinary case, because they choose their own signer — it reads the COMPANY's name within 80 characters of a cue and a date within 240, marked `unsure`, and the person filing confirms it. **FILING NEEDS EVERY SIGNATURE** (`signedCopy.everyone === true`, asked by the server): a copy one party has signed is recorded as part-signed and the file keeps waiting.

**FOUND BY DRIVING THE PAGE, NOT BY READING IT.**
- The 25 Sep signing copy painted "Sign here" tabs on the paper of a contract nobody signs in HaTi — a promise the product cannot keep. `wireDocCanvas` asks `_theySign` before painting places to sign or their flags.
- The head offered "Add signers". `wsNextAction` has the route's own two acts now: Hand over for signing (`ho-hand`) and File the signed copy (`ho-file`).
- The Signing order card said "EMAIL FAILED" and "their turn" beside our own signatory: the server was trying to tell somebody it was their turn on a route that has no turns. `notifyInternalSignerTurn` answers `they-sign`, and the card draws no turn and no notice.
- "Accept as signed" filed a copy not everybody had signed. It is "accept-partial" now — the difference recorded, the file still waiting — and the server refuses the filing without `everyone === true`.
- `portalHandedOver` was drawn by the counterparty's page and not published, so the browser probe read `undefined` — f232's class again; it is published first.
- The day's full run found the handover mail reading the Overview's "Who else" list. The 21 Sep wall says naming somebody there sends them nothing, and f354 greps the server for the word: the line is gone and the server never reads that list. The mail goes to the lead, the desk, the signatory and whoever approved.
- The "another way" key was `ho_via_other`, and the book's plural check read it as half of a pair. It is `ho_via_else`; the stored value `other` is a record value and did not move.
- **TWO MORE ON THE LAST READ-THROUGH OF MY OWN DIFF.** The wall counted a WITHDRAWN approval request as an approval (`srvMayAcceptDiffer`), where the browser's own reading counts only one that was given — so the named approver of a request that was taken back could accept a copy whose words differ. Approved only now, and f388 7k2 evaluates the function itself off the server's source (red before). And the upload's recognition compared the first twenty files out in whatever order the list held them and offered the first forty in its pick-list — a twenty-first file out was never recognised and a forty-first could not be chosen at all, in silence. `HO_MATCH_MAX` (20) is named, the likeliest are compared first (their company named in the text, then the newest handover), and the pick-list names every file out; f388 (10) drives it with 45 files out (both red before).

- **THE BROWSER SET FOUND ONE MORE, AND IT WAS A LAYOUT RULE.** The admin's default answer to "who runs the signing?" was built as a settings row of its own in The agreement group, which made that group five long and the tab eighteen rows — and the settings page's own rule, measured by settings-groups-verify, is that no group is a wall (1c: the largest holds four; 1d: the seventeen, once each). Adding a sixth group is the owner's call, so the setting moved INTO the drawer of the rule it sits beside, "The check before signing" — the same kind of rule, how a contract gets to signed — under its own heading, and a panel may now carry `find`: words the settings search reads, so "who runs" still finds it. Driven: the search finds it, the press saves it, the server reads it back.

**MORE THAN TWO PARTIES (Phase 2).** Every party that negotiates must agree, and where more than one did, one Ready to sign from one link cannot speak for the others — so the window asks each one's agreement by name and day (`srvPartiesNegotiating` on the server), the file goes to each, and filing expects every signing party.

**THE UPLOAD RECOGNISES A SIGNED COPY (decision 9).** The ordinary Upload button compares what it read with every file out for signature (`outsideMatchUpload`, `HO_MATCH_MIN` 0.6) and ASKS — "this looks like the signed copy of RL-012" — never assumes; below the bar it offers a pick-list of the files out. Their link is not a door: a copy arriving there could be anybody's.

**THE FIVE FAULTS THE DESIGN NAMED IN TODAY'S PAPER FILING, PUT RIGHT.** "Signed on paper instead? File the signed copy here" on the Signing tab was a small version of this route, and the design listed what it got wrong. (1) The signed copy was stored and no screen could open it again — the filed record now carries the signed copy of record, and it opens. (2) The record said the contract was migrated and showed the file uploaded at the START; the evidence pack said the same — both now name the signed copy (`outsideExecutionBlock`, drawn for a contract filed through the old door too, which kept its file on `execution` and never showed it). (3) Verify reported a problem with the seal on every contract filed that way — the v3 seal binds the signed copy's own fingerprint and `verifySeal` re-hashes the stored file. (4) It read nothing from the signed copy, so the days it was signed never reached the record — `outsideReadCopy` reads them and the person filing confirms them. (5) It asked only whether the negotiation was settled and whether a named person's approval was waiting, skipping the value approvals, the checks and the brief, and the server asked nothing — the door now SWITCHES THE ROUTE (the same words, "Signed on paper instead?", press `outsideSetRoute(c,'outside')`), every one of those is asked at the handover on the server, and the server refuses a signed copy on any file that was not handed over (`handoverNeeded`). `openPaperSignatureModal` has no caller now. And one the 24 Sep note logged: "Send signed copies" attached the unsigned original; `executedAttachment` sends the signed copy.

**THE CHECKS THIS WORK MOVED, IN PLACE.** Eight were byte counts or a pinned expression that the new branches pushed past, and each was re-pointed to the REGION or the RELATION with the reason beside it: f224 (the evidence pack, a 4,200-character slice → the function), f240 (1) (the alert row prints `a.ref||a.id`), f273 8b (the decline dialog's fallback is the reference), f308 (5b) (a THIRD signing door — the handover asks `signCheckRefusal` — so the count is four, and a claim that it asks before anything leaves), f335 (8) (the status dot's region), f348 (4c) (the calendar's label), f383 (5A) (no places to sign on a contract they sign), f51 (the issue-signing act inside the block its predicate opens). Two were answered in the CODE and the checks were left alone: f289 (39) counts the lock rule's name, and a comment of mine had named it a third time; f381 (6) pins the quiet desk beside the negotiation, so the handover alert sits after the quiet desk. f148 gained `ho_via_docusign` ("DocuSign") and `ho_sig_named` ("{who} · {title}") on SAME_IN_BOTH.

**PRE-EXISTING RED, LEFT RED**: f277 (1) and (10) and f387 (2e) and (4c) fail identically on unmodified main.

**NOT BUILT, said out loud**: the phone offers neither act (it says to do it on a computer); the server's full-text search (the palette's "In the wording" rows) does not find a contract by its number — the number is not in that index, and a hyphen is stripped before a word is asked — while the Contracts search, the palette's own contract rows and Copilot do; the value-rule approval chain is written by the browser and the server neither computes it nor guards who marks a step approved — the handover asks the STORED chain, the in-app signature does not ask it at all (logged, not widened).

**THE GATES.** Lint 0 errors, one warning fewer than main (`srvPartiesNegotiating` is used now). The node suite: every failure left is one main fails identically — f277 (1) and (10), f387 (2e) and (4c). f388: 51 claims, all 51 red at the parent. redline-here-sign-there-verify: 29 checks, 28 red at the parent — the one that passes is the staging line (the upload dialog reads a file on both), and the file is GUARDED: where the walk stops, every check it did not reach is reported by name, read off the file's own calls, and a missing control costs five seconds rather than the driver's thirty. The whole browser set: 151 files, 44 red on the branch; the 44 run again on main's code — 43 red there with the same failures word for word, and the 44th was settings-groups (above), 33/33 after the move. The colour census's output is byte-identical to main's.


### A FILE THEY SIGN HAS NO BLANKS FOR US TO FILL (Young, 26 Sep 2026)

Off a screenshot of an uploaded commercial lease, the Document tab's right-hand column showing *Blanks in this document · 0 of 29*: *"if the contract is being signed out of hati and the contract is simply being used to negotiate the clauses, these fields are irrelevant I would presume."*

**MEASURED BEFORE A LINE MOVED, AND THE PRESUMPTION WAS RIGHT FOR A REASON THE PANEL ALREADY SAID.** On the outside route what they receive is the agreed WORDING as a Word file, built from `outsideAgreedHtml` — the negotiation's resolved body, else the stored wording, else the extracted text. Not one of those reads `c.fields`, which is where an answer to an uploaded document's blank is kept, and the panel's own heading says so on its hover (*"Your answers are kept on this record. The document they sent is not changed."*). So on that route a reader could fill in all twenty-nine boxes and hand over a file carrying none of them. A form whose answers go nowhere is worse than no form.

**THE SCREENSHOT'S OWN CONTRACT WAS NOT ON THAT ROUTE**: its sub-line printed MK-438, and a working file prints RL-### until its signed copy is filed. Its title — *RL-001-agreed* — is the file name the handover gives the agreed words, uploaded again as a new contract, on the default route. Said to the owner, because the panel still draws on that contract and will until its route is switched.

**ONE READING, ONE GATE.** `uploadBlanksTheirs(c)` (js/uploadblanks.js, published) is an upload whose route is `outside` — `signRouteOf`, with the literal as the fallback because js/outside.js is not on every stage. `uploadBlanksLive` asks it, and every reader of upload blanks already asks that gate: the panel (`renderBlankFormSection`, through `contractHasBlanks`), the marks (`uploadBlanksPaint`, which clears before it asks, so a repaint after a route switch takes them off), the counts and the arrival read's fill step. **A DRAFTED CONTRACT ON THAT ROUTE KEEPS ITS BLANKS** — its answers are written into our own paper, which is what gets handed over.

**THE TILE HAD TO BE TOLD, OR IT WOULD HAVE LIED.** With the gate shut, `contractBlanksNone` fell through to `upload`, whose sentence is *"HaTi cannot read its blanks yet"* — false: it can, and on this route it does not ask. A fifth reason, `theirs`, is asked before that one, with its own head (`tri_t_fill_theirs`, "Open fields are theirs to fill") and sentence (`tri_fill_theirs`), steel and never a tick. **AND THE TILE ASKS THE ROUTE LIVE, BOTH WAYS**: the route can move after the arrival reading ran (until the handover it is one press on the Signing tab), and the panel beside the tile asks it live. An older note that counted twenty-nine open blanks stops counting them once the contract is theirs to sign; a recorded `theirs` is not believed once it has been switched back, and the blanks are counted as they stand.

**A READING, NEVER A DELETE**: answers already typed stay on the record, and the browser check switches the route back through the route card's own link and finds the panel, every mark and the kept answer where they were left. **THE HANDOVER'S OWN CHECK IS A DIFFERENT QUESTION AND IS UNTOUCHED**: a placeholder written into the agreed words (`[insert amount]`, `[COMPANY NAME]`, `{{key}}`) still holds the handover (`outsideBlanksOf`), because whatever is in the file is what they sign. Ruled lines like the lease's `[______]` never did.

Tests: f342 sections (7) and (8) — 14 claims, 11 red at the parent (f4d1604); 7g and 8d are CONTROLS, 7h a WALL. 8e was added on the last read-through: what Copilot filled before a route switch stays named, and only the open count — a claim about now — goes. upload-blanks-verify section 9 presses the Signing tab's own door (`#sign-paper`, then `#cf-ok`) on the document section 1 measured — 3 of 10 red at the parent, which prints *"5 boxes · heading Blanks in this document"*; 9a is the GATE and six are CONTROLS that hold on both sides. f347 (3d) re-pointed in place: it pinned `fl.left` by spelling, and the count now rides in `left` so the route reading can correct it.


### A BLANK THEY FILLED IN IS NOT A CHANGE (Young ruled 26 Sep 2026: "yes, accept the filled-in blanks without asking")

The morning's work had found it and logged it: a ruled blank in the agreed words that the other side filled in their copy — the date line, the name line, the lease's `[______]` — read as changed wording in the filing word check, one changed paragraph per blank, so a perfectly ordinary signed copy could only be filed by the approver or an admin with a reason. Asked whether HaTi should accept those or keep asking, the owner answered in eight words.

**MEASURED FIRST.** A ruled line is zero words to the check (an underscore is not a letter), so a filled date line read as the agreed words plus three new ones on the same line — the "words added on the same line are part of the clause" rule, working as written. A bracketed placeholder was worse: "[Customer name]" is two agreed words, so filling it read as two struck and three added. Run through the real filing screen on the commit before this work, a supply agreement with three blanks came back *"3 differences from the agreed wording"* with only *File with the difference* and *Hold* to press.

**WHAT A BLANK IS, IS ALREADY WRITTEN DOWN — ONCE.** The upload panel (js/uploadblanks.js) has read the blanks in a document somebody sent us since 20 Sep: three text shapes, a Word box, their refusals and their names. The word check asks the SAME reader (`upHits`, `upLabel`, `upLead`) through the global rather than growing a second copy of its patterns, so the blanks HaTi showed on their document are the blanks whose fills it accepts, called what the panel called them. It is narrowed by the handover's own reading — a bracket that names itself ("[Reserved]", "[Signature]", "[Schedule 2]") is not a blank, because putting words in its place IS a change. The panel is a browser module and the check runs only in the browser that read the file; where the panel's reader is not loaded, nothing is read as a blank and a fill reads as a change, which is the old answer and asks a person (f389 2h is that control).

**HOW A FILL IS TOLD FROM A CHANGE.** A blank is taken OUT of the agreed paragraph's words and kept as a gap — how many words come before it (`ohChunksBlanks`). Everything that finds a paragraph in their copy is untouched: a ruled line already contributed no words, and a placeholder's own words were never agreed wording. After the word-by-word alignment, a run of THEIR words that strikes none of OURS, standing exactly at a gap that carries a blank, and no longer than the blanks there can hold (`OH_FILL_MAX`, twenty words a blank — a blank holds a fact, a date, a name, an address, not a clause), is a fill (`ohFillOps`): its steps become `'f'`, read as kept by every reading below it, and it is listed. A placeholder they left exactly as it was is simply the agreed wording and is not listed. A paragraph with a real change and a fill in it marks only the change. Pass 2's search window is widened by what the blanks can hold, or a long address in the middle of a clause would push the clause's own last words out of the window. The leading-numbering allowance (their "14." on our "1.") stands down where a blank opens the paragraph: the words there are what was written in it.

**A LINE THAT IS ONLY A BLANK** has no words to be found by, so it is not a paragraph; it keeps its place in the order and is pinned by its NEIGHBOURS — the words lying in their copy exactly between the two agreed paragraphs around it, both found, in the agreed order, with nothing else found between them. The first build accepted a sentence written on a bare signature line as a fill; driven on purpose, that is the obvious smuggle. So only a NAMED blank is pinned this way — a bare ruled line is a line to sign on, not a blank to write in — and a blank holds one line: a second line written under a named one is text they added (f389 2e, 2f).

**THE WORD BOX.** The one shape the text cannot show. `outsideAgreedParas` reads each `span.hati-wfield` off the agreed markup and hands it to the check by its own words (`fields`); an empty box — Word pads it with spaces, which the text collapses away — reads as a ruled line, which is what it is on the page. Driven in the test world: a box still saying "Click or tap here to enter text." typed over with the buyer's name is a fill named "Buyer name", the name its file gave it.

**THEIR COPY IS NEVER READ FOR BLANKS.** A bracket they added to a clause ("[subject to board approval]") is words they added, and stays a change (f389 2g).

**ACCEPTED WITHOUT ASKING, NEVER WITHOUT SAYING.** The fills are listed — open — under the result on both screens that show the check (the check before our signatory signs, and the filing screen), each blank by its name and what their copy says there. The record line says "N blanks filled in." whichever way the words went, so the trail lines written at the check and at filing carry it. The filing record keeps the count and the first thirty (`signedCopy.compare.filled` / `fills`), which the evidence pack takes whole, and the signed record's "Same as the agreed version" cell counts them.

**THE SIX QUESTIONS CHANGED ONE THING**: the cheapest channel for "what was accepted" is a line in the result card already there, not a new panel; the list is open because it is what the person filing is implicitly accepting when they press File. No band; the contract's paper is not on this screen.

**NOT COVERED, SAID.** A fill that starts on its paragraph's line and wraps onto the next line of a PDF reads its tail as text added between clauses (the safe direction). A signing service's stamp printed on a bare signature line INSIDE the agreement reads as it always did. And one found on the way and handed to the owner rather than widened: the handover's own placeholder check refuses `[insert …]`, `[ALL CAPS]` and `{{key}}` but not `[amount]` or `[Price]` — its own comment's example is one it does not catch — so such a blank can reach them unfilled, and filled by them it is now accepted and listed. Before today it would have come back flagged.

Tests: f389 — 26 claims, 16 red against the commit before this work (e2d34ea), and the ten marked WALL or CONTROL pass on both sides on purpose; a list born inside the test world is compared as text (the realm rule). redline-here-sign-there-verify section 8 — a second working file with three blanks, handed over through the real window, the signed copy through Upload's own recognition: 8a0–8e red at the parent, which prints *"3 differences from the agreed wording"* and offers File with the difference and Hold; the two stage lines pass on both. The section-4 staging was lifted into a helper so the second file settles the same list the first did.

## THE INSPECTOR ON FOUR MORE PAGES — OBLIGATIONS, THE CONTRACT'S TAB, OUR STANDARDS, REQUESTS (Young chose it for each, 26 Sep 2026)

**THE ORDER.** Over one working day the owner looked at the Inspector on Contracts, Negotiations and Approvals, then asked for a render of the Obligations page "keeping the same format as the inspector design" with two rivals, asked how the reminders in the drawing are set up, chose Inspector for the page and then for the contract's Obligations tab, asked for all three tabs of Our standards in the same design, and chose Inspector for the Requests page over two rivals. "Yes to all three" answered the three Requests rulings; "I want to build all the pages in one go. Summarize what we have agreed on to build" then "go and merge main when complete". The approved picture is the artifact "Obligations, Standards, Requests".

**THE FRAME WAS WIDENED, NOT COPIED.** The panel had only ever described a contract. `insPaintPanel` gained `item` beside `c` — a head (`insItemHeadHtml`, the same five rows in the same classes, the title allowed two lines because an obligation or a standard is named in a sentence) and a body the caller builds — and `host`, because the contract's tab draws its panel inside the room. `insActsHtml` was lifted out of the contract head byte for byte so every panel's verbs are one builder; `insChipHtml` / `insViewTabsHtml` are the register's own chip and view tab, so `.reg-filterbar`'s clothes dress them and selectMenuSweep draws HaTi's list. The header's facts line and filled act had one precedent (the register's `#reg-head-facts`); `PAGE_HEAD_PAINT` made it a table so three more pages could fill the header's two slots after the view paints (the header paints AFTER the view — a painter that ran only in the view would paint slots that did not exist yet).

**OBLIGATIONS — THE ONE POPULATION.** The page counted each view by walking the book once per view; `obwBook()` reads allObligations once, each row finding its contract in a map built once (the performance audit's lesson), and `obwPass(o, f)` is every filter as one predicate. f255 pinned obwRows' body for the names it borrows; the claim is unchanged and is asked of the three functions now.
- **A HELD STEP WAS OVERDUE ON THE PAGE AND WAITING EVERYWHERE ELSE.** The Overdue view asked obState; the sidebar door and the group heading asked the band. MEASURED: a door reading 2 opened a list of 3. The view asks the window now.
- **"NOBODY OWNS IT" WAS FILLED WITH ROWS NOBODY COULD OWN.** The old cut was "no reminder reaches anybody", which included every obligation of theirs. The chip says ownership, and the Whose cell of a theirs row names the other side. f255 (2) is reversed in place with the reason.
- **MONEY IS NEVER NETTED.** What we owe, what we are owed, what we paid and what we received are four sums, each through the same converter; one total would be a number that means nothing.
- **THE REMINDERS SECTION IS THE SWEEP'S OWN RULES, SAID.** The owner asked how the drawing's reminders are set up; the answer was runReminders, and the panel says exactly that: seven days before, the day, the day after to the person the mail reaches, the admins four days late; a theirs obligation or one nobody resolves reaches the admins the day after; a held step fires nothing until the step before it is done; no date, never.
- Kept that the drawing took off, said: Mark done stays drawn (plain) on a theirs obligation and on a waiting step, because taking it off would remove a way to record a fact the product accepts today.

**OUR STANDARDS — THE LINKS ARE THE FEATURE.** Three tabs that had never pointed at each other: a standard now lists the contracts that depart from it, a book lists where its contracts depart, and a departure opens the standard it misses — each a press on the tab's own button, so the classic page's one handler (class and hidden flips, never a rebuild — f272's wall) still answers every tab change.
- **"LIABILITY CAP" WAS TWO CHIPS ON TWO BOOKS.** resolvePlaybook returns positions and ranges separately and the page drew both. `stdBookLines` folds them by name.
- **THE LEASE BOOK'S OWN STANDARD READ AS INHERITED** on the first build: its positions are a getter that hands back new objects on every read, so an identity test called its stamp duty "from the baseline". `own` is asked by name.
- **THE DEVIATIONS TAB SHOWED THE TOP EIGHT OF TWENTY AND SAID NOTHING OF THE REST.** It lists every contract with a departure, grouped by whether it can still change (`stdOpenToChange`: not signed and no signature on either side).
- **THE SENTENCE UNDER A BOOK IS THE RULE THAT CHOOSES IT.** playbookKeyFor's four inline patterns became `PB_TYPE_PATTERNS`; the rule compiles them and the panel prints them (`pbTypeWords`, a stem spelled for a reader through `PB_STEM_SAYS`). The pattern strings are written out whole because f133 holds the server's mirror to the same text; f390 (4f) holds the rule to every key it answered before.
- **A SAVE FROM THE PANEL LANDS ON THE PANEL.** Every save on this page ends in renderClauseLibrary or renderPlaybookView, whose hosts do not exist in the Inspector's shape; both now repaint the page when it is mounted. The classic book row's Remove and Reset were lifted out word for word into `pbRemoveType` / `pbResetPlaybook` so both shapes press one act. Removing a STANDARD asks first on the Inspector (the classic row's own Remove, which does not ask, is left exactly as it was and is logged).
- **THE FIRST-READ OFFER IS THE CLASSIC CARD CONDENSED, NOT A NEW BAND.** Where the workspace still runs on the default playbook and enough signed paper exists to compare (`stdDraftWorthOffering`, the classic card's own test), the Inspector draws the same heading as one line with Compare them — the full comparison, `renderStandardsDraft`, in a window (`sdOpenDraftCompare`) — and Leave them as they are, which puts it away for the sitting. Nothing it offered was lost; it takes a line where the card took a screen.

**REQUESTS — THE PAGE USED A THIRD OF THE SCREEN.** A column of cards 894px wide became the list and the panel, from two chairs: the team that drafts, and the colleague who only asks.
- **A HELD REQUEST SAID "WAITING".** Its status stays `open` — holding moves who has it, not where it has got to — so the page and the tracker link told the person who asked that nobody had picked it up while a colleague was working on it. `intakeStatusKey` is the one reading, and the tracker asks the same two columns. Derived, never stored; it sends no mail.
- **PICK IT UP TOOK IT FROM A COLLEAGUE IN SILENCE.** On a row somebody else held, the one control moved it to the presser and the colleague found out from the queue. It is named for what it does now — Take it over — and it asks.
- **THE HELPING SENTENCE MOVED INTO THE ASK WINDOW**, where the person asking reads it before they type.

**WHAT WAS MEASURED.** Each page driven in a real browser at 1440 and at 1000 (the classic shape, byte for byte what it was), both Requests chairs, the take-over question, both remove questions, the tracker page, the width watch in both directions. Four older browser files measure the classic shape and now stage it with insForce(false); their failures match the parent's exactly (obligations-tab-verify's band heading and amount-and-window-verify's "sel.options is not iterable" are red at the parent too).
